title: The Fathers on Jeremiah
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: The Seventy's "The word of God which came upon Jeremiah" differs from the Hebrew "Words of Jeremiah", which suits a prophet who, mocked for saying "Thus says the Lord", called God's words his own so that people would listen.
comments.comment:
… Jeremiah came to be in times of people most sinful—for in his days the captivity came to be—and they were so sinful as to sneer and laugh and mock whenever the prophet spoke the prophetic opening, 'Thus says the Lord.' The hearers laughed and sneered at what was said. The one deceived and benefited from being deceived [Jeremiah] guarded himself from saying 'Thus says the Lord.' Therefore he also, wanting to deceive for benefit from deceiving, said: I speak my own words to you, since you do not hear the Lord’s words. Then they offered their ears as to words of Jeremiah and heard words of God. These things the one who handed the place over to me said, examining the openings and beginnings of the prophecies.

There is then also a beginning of Jeremiah’s prophecy among us, as the Seventy have handed down—I do not know with what aim: 'The word of God which came upon Jeremiah the son of Hilkiah from the priests' (Jeremiah 1:1); but in the Hebrew and the remaining editions: 'Words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah,' … and all agreed to say: 'Words of Jeremiah son of Hilkiah.' Why then 'Words of Jeremiah'? Because his opening toward those not wanting to hear was: Hear my words.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the book is headed "Words of Jeremiah".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dates of Jeremiah's prophecy are not mere history, because the reader who attends to the reading is taught something through them.
comments.comment:
You will find the same thing in what is written about Jeremiah. The time of his prophecy is recorded: when he began, and how far he prophesied. Then the reader, if he does not attend to the reading and examine the intent of the passages set down, will say: this is history, and it is written when Jeremiah began to prophesy, and after how long a time he stopped. What is this history to me?

I read, and I learned that he began to prophesy 'in the days of Josiah son of Amos, king of Judah, in the thirteenth year of his reign.' (Jeremiah 1:2) Then 'it came to pass in the days of Jehoiakim son of Josiah, king of Judah,' (Jeremiah 1:3) and he prophesied 'until the end of the eleventh year of Zedekiah son of Josiah, king of Judah.' And I learned that his prophecy stretched through three kings, 'until the captivity of Jerusalem in the fifth month.' What then are we taught through these things, if we attend to the reading?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God sent Jeremiah before the captivity and into it so that those who heard might repent, and the same love urges us, who also become captives when we sin.
comments.comment:
God condemned Jerusalem for her sins, and they had been judged to be left to captivity. Even so the God who loves mankind, when the time had come, sends this prophet also, starting two reigns before the captivity, so that those who were willing, taking it in, might repent through the prophetic words. He sent a prophet to prophesy under the second king after the first, and under the third, up to the very times of the captivity.

For the long-suffering God was giving a delay even, so to speak, one day before the captivity, urging those who heard to repent, so that the grim things of the captivity might cease. That is why it is written that Jeremiah prophesied 'until the captivity of Jerusalem, until the fifth month.' (Jeremiah 1:3) He had begun, and he was still prophesying, as if to say: you have become captives; even so, repent. If you repent, the captivity will not go on, but the mercy of God will stand over you.

So we have something useful from the record that gives the times of the prophecy: that God, according to his own love of mankind, urges those who hear not to suffer the things of the captivity. It is like this with us too. If we sin, we also are about to become captives. For 'to hand such a one over to Satan' (1 Corinthians 5:5) differs in nothing from handing those from Jerusalem over to Nebuchadnezzar. As they were handed over to him because of sins, so we are handed over to Satan because of sins — Satan who is a Nebuchadnezzar. And 'those I handed over to Satan, that they may be taught not to blaspheme,' (1 Timothy 1:20) the apostle says of other sinners.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God sent the prophet up to the very time of the captivity.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah received a gift set apart from the other prophets: God said to him alone that he knew and sanctified him before birth.
comments.comment:
After the preface it is written that 'the word of the Lord came to him' (Jeremiah 1:4) — clearly, to Jeremiah. And what does the word of the Lord say to him? Something set apart from what was said to the other prophets. For we have found this said to none of the prophets.

Abraham was called a prophet in the word, 'He is a prophet, and he will pray for you,' (Genesis 20:7) and God did not say to him, 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you.' (Jeremiah 1:5) Abraham was sanctified later, when he went out from his land and from his kindred and from his father's house. Isaac was born of promise, and we have not found this word said even to him. Why should I go through the rest? Jeremiah received a gift set apart: 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you.' (Jeremiah 1:5)
comments.selected_reason: Explains what is special in the words God speaks to Jeremiah.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture says "formed" rather than "made" of the body in the womb, and God knows only those who are worthy of his knowledge.
comments.comment:
Whether it is said to Jeremiah or to the Savior, 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you' (Jeremiah 1:5): if you read Genesis and watch what is said about the making of the world, you will find that the Scripture, with a very fine distinction, did not say, 'Before I made you in the womb I know you.' (Genesis 1:26) For when the one according to the image was being created, 'God said, Let us make man according to our image and likeness.' He did not say, Let us form. But when he took 'dust from the earth,' he did not make the man; he 'formed the man,' and 'placed in the garden the man whom he had formed, to work it and to keep it.' (Genesis 2:15)

If you can, see the difference between making and forming. The Lord, whether to Jeremiah or to the Savior, did not say, 'Before I made you in the womb I know you.' (Jeremiah 1:5) For what is made does not come about in the womb; what is formed from the dust of the earth is created in the womb. 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you.' (Jeremiah 1:5) If the Lord knew all, he would not have said to Jeremiah as something set apart, 'I know you.' So God knows those who matter, God knows those worthy of his knowledge, and 'the Lord knew those who are his.' Those unworthy God does not know, as the Savior also does not: 'I never knew you.'

We, being men, as we advance, judge some things worthy of our knowing them. Some things we do not even want to hear, so that we may not know them. Some things we want to know. What of the God of all? Does he want to know Pharaoh? Does he want to know the Egyptians? They are not worthy of the knowledge of God. Moses is worthy, and each of the prophets of that rank. You must set many things right before God begins to know you. Jeremiah he knew before forming him in the womb.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the particular wording "I formed you" and "I know you".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God sanctified Jeremiah before he came out of the womb, not waiting for his birth.
comments.comment: How does he say, 'Before I formed you in the womb I know you, and before you came out of the womb I have sanctified you' (Jeremiah 1:5)? God sanctifies some for himself. He did not wait for this one to come into birth in order to sanctify him; he had already sanctified him before he came out of the womb. If you refer it to the Savior, it is not hard to say that he has been sanctified before coming out of the womb. If you refer it to the Savior, he has been sanctified not only before coming out, but still earlier. This Jeremiah was sanctified before coming out of the womb.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah was set as a prophet to the nations as the letter shows when he prophesied against them, and the higher sense is that the Savior truly prophesies to all nations.
comments.comment:
'I have set you as a prophet to the nations.' (Jeremiah 1:5) If you look for this in Jeremiah — 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5) — watch later on: he is commanded to prophesy 'against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 25:15) and there is a heading, 'What Jeremiah prophesied against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 25:13) against Elam, against Damascus, against Moab. And we have it that he 'prophesied against all the nations,' (Jeremiah 25:13) as regards the letter of 'I have set you as a prophet to the nations,' (Jeremiah 1:5) said to him.

If it is a matter of the higher sense: if of Jeremiah, we have already spoken; if of the Savior, what need is there even to say it? He truly prophesied to all the nations. For he is, as he is ten thousand other things, also a prophet. As he is high priest, as he is savior, as he is physician, so he is also prophet. Moses, prophesying about him, did not say only 'a prophet,' but said it with a special force: 'The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from your brothers, like me (Deuteronomy 18:15); him you shall hear, and it shall be that whoever does not hear that prophet shall be destroyed from his people.' (Acts 3:23)

This one, then, is also the prophet set 'to the nations,' and he received grace from God poured out on his lips, so that not only when he was present in the body, but also now, when he is present in power and in the Spirit, he may prophesy 'to all the nations,' so that from all the nations his prophecy may reach its end and draw men to salvation (Acts 3:22–23) (Psalm 45:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Jeremiah was 'a prophet unto the nations' and how the words reach further.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah was sanctified before birth and appointed a prophet, as Paul and others were chosen before the foundation of the world.
comments.comment: Again Jeremiah hears: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the womb I sanctified you, and I appointed you a prophet to the nations' (Jeremiah 1:5). Before coming forth from the womb he was sanctified, and as a prophet to the nations he was appointed. Again: 'Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world' (Ephesians 1:4). By 'foundation of the world' he means his coming-to-be. And Paul and those with him were chosen before the foundation of the world, and this election has become theirs from then until now, so that they might be sent out together with those who have been called and might be able to help them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Jeremiah's words "I am younger" can fit the Savior if, like the child of Isaiah, he advanced in wisdom and stature and chose the good before he knew evil.
comments.comment:
Here, at what seems ill-sounding as regards the Savior, work the word somehow: how can the Savior say, 'I do not know how to speak, because I am younger,' (Jeremiah 1:6) and the rest? You see that the argument is in a tight place. …

How then can we refer these things to the Savior? Bring the Old Covenant as a witness: 'Before the child knows good or evil, he refuses evil to choose the good.' (Isaiah 7:15–16) And these things are said outright about the Savior in Isaiah: 'Behold, the virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel.' (Isaiah 7:14) And there it is added: 'before the child knows.' (Isaiah 7:16) And if an example must also be taken from the gospel: Jesus, not yet become a man but still a child, since 'he emptied himself,' was advancing. For no one who is already perfected advances; he advances who still needs advance. So he 'advanced in stature, advanced in wisdom, advanced in grace with God and men.' If he emptied himself coming down here, and emptying himself was taking again from what he had emptied himself of, having emptied himself willingly, what is strange if he also advanced 'in wisdom and stature and grace with God and men,' (Luke 2:52) and if what I set down from Isaiah is true of him: before he knows good or evil he will choose the good and refuse evil?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Savior's "I do not know how to speak" is great because speaking is human, and as the Word with God he knows what is greater than speaking.
comments.comment: How will you show that it is a great and glorious thing for the Savior to say, 'I do not know how to speak' (Jeremiah 1:6)? Speaking is a human thing. To speak is to use a dialect: the speech of the Hebrews, say, or of the Greeks, or of some others. If you go up to the Savior and see him as Word 'in the beginning with God,' (John 1:1) you will see that he does not know how to speak, because speaking is human. He does not know it, because what he knows is greater than speaking. And if you compare the tongues of angels with the tongues of men, and see that he is greater even than angels, as the apostle bore witness in the letter to the Hebrews, you will say that he was greater even than the tongue of angels when he was God, the Word with the Father.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah was a child in body but a grown man within, and God tells him not to fear the faces of hearers who will persecute him as they do every prophet.
comments.comment:
'And I said, You who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak, because I am younger. And the Lord said to me, Do not say that I am younger, because to all to whom I send you...' (Jeremiah 1:6–8) We have often said that it is possible, according to the inner man, to be a child, even if someone is in an old age of body. And it is possible at times, according to the outer man, to be a child, and according to the inner, a man. Such was Jeremiah, already having the grace from God while he was still in the age of a child according to the body. That is why the Lord says to him, 'Do not say that I am younger.' (Jeremiah 1:7) And a sign that he is not younger, but 'a grown man,' is this: 'To all to whom I send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their face.' (Matthew 13:57)

The Word of God knows that those who serve as ambassadors of the word are in danger among the hearers. For when they are exposed they hate them; when they are rebuked they persecute them. The prophets suffer every kind of thing. 'A prophet is not without honor except in his own country and in his house' (Matthew 13:57) — which we also recalled earlier. So God, sending the prophet, knows how many dangers he will take on, and he says to him, 'Do not be afraid of their face, because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 1:8)

What Jeremiah suffered is written down. He was thrown into a pit of mire; he remained there eating one loaf a day and drinking water only; and ten thousand other things which his prophecy has made clear. 'Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute?' (Acts 7:52) it is said to the Jews. And it is necessary that 'those who want to live in a godly way in Christ Jesus be persecuted in every case by opposing powers, through the vessels they find.' (2 Timothy 3:12) Therefore those who are persecuted must not be surprised, but must do everything, only praying that they be persecuted unjustly and not justly — not for injustice, not for sin, not for greed. And if someone is ever persecuted for righteousness, let him also hear, 'Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every evil word against you, lying, for my sake (Matthew 5:11). Rejoice and be glad, because your reward is great in the heavens; for so they persecuted the prophets who were before you.' (Matthew 5:10–12) (2 Corinthians 4:16)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God says "Do not say, I am younger" and "Do not be afraid of their face".
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Some refer these words to the Savior, but because some of them cannot fit him the whole connected run of words should be referred to Jeremiah and the greater things interpreted.
comments.comment:
We are not unaware that some refer these words, as greater than Jeremiah, to our Savior and Lord. And one must know that much of it agrees with him and can be referred to the Savior — I will set that out. But a few of the things said to Jeremiah press the argument, and cannot, as most people take them, be fitted to the Savior.

What then fits the Savior? 'To all to whom I send you, you shall go, and according to all that I command you, you shall speak. Do not be afraid of their face, because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 1:7–8) These would not yet clearly seem to be referred to the Savior. But what follows puts the reading about Jeremiah in a tight place: 'And the Lord stretched out his hand toward me and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me, Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down.' (Jeremiah 1:9–10) What nations did Jeremiah uproot? What kingdoms did he overthrow? For it is written, 'Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down.' (Jeremiah 1:10) And what authority did Jeremiah have 'to destroy'? And whom did he build in such numbers that it should be said 'and to build'? Jeremiah says, 'I have not profited, and no one has profited me.' (Jeremiah 15:10) How then is 'to build and to plant' given to him? How will 'to plant' fit Jeremiah?

These things, referred to the Savior, do not press the interpreter, because in them Jeremiah is a symbol of the Savior. But what I am about to set down presses even the most intelligent person who wants to show how these too can fit the Savior: 'And I said, You who are, Master, Lord, behold, I do not know how to speak.' (Jeremiah 1:6) He who is Wisdom, he who is the Power of God, who brought us 'the fullness of the deity, which dwelt in him bodily' (Colossians 2:9) — how then can 'I do not know how to speak' fit the Savior? And 'I am younger' is forbidden to the Savior, as if he were saying it wrongly. For if the Lord says to him, Do not say this, it is clear that he forbids what is not well said. So these do not fit the Savior. Those other words do not seem to put the Savior to shame.

To say that these belong to Jeremiah and those to the Savior is not hard. But a fair-minded person will be much pressed here. To cut a connected run of words, and to say, 'These, being lesser, fit Jeremiah and not Christ, and these, being greater than Jeremiah, fit Christ and not Jeremiah' — that is the work of people without judgment. Let the whole, then, be referred to Jeremiah, and let even the things that seem greater than Jeremiah be interpreted.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord gives words to uproot, which the Word in the Father had no need of, and "I do not know how to speak" is as great a saying as "I do not know you".
comments.comment:
'Do not say, I am younger, because to all to whom I send you, you shall go.' (Jeremiah 1:7) So he stretches out the hand, touches his mouth, and gives him words, and gives him words because of the kingdoms, that he may uproot. When he was 'in the Father' he had no need of words that uproot. He had no words that pull down and take apart the worse things. For nothing there was worthy of being pulled down, nothing worthy of being uprooted.

It is a great thing, as 'I do not know you, because you are workers of lawlessness' (Matthew 7:23) is a great thing, said by the Savior because of the surpassing greatness of his glory. Equal in force to 'I do not know how to speak human things' (John 14:10) is this 'I do not know how to speak.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah was sanctified from the womb, so no seraph's coal as with Isaiah but the Lord's own hand touched his mouth.
comments.comment: 'Because I am with you to deliver you, says the Lord. And the Lord stretched out his hand toward me, and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me.' (Jeremiah 1:8–10) Watch the difference between Jeremiah and Isaiah. Isaiah says, 'I have unclean lips, and I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen the King, the Lord of hosts, with my eyes.' (Isaiah 6:5) And since he confessed that he did not have unclean works, but only small words (for to that point he was a sinner), the Lord did not stretch out his hand. One of the seraphim touched his lips with his hand, and said, 'Behold, I have taken away your iniquities.' (Isaiah 6:6–7) But because this one was sanctified 'from the womb,' no tongs are sent to him, and no coal 'from the altar' (he had nothing worthy of the fire). The Lord's own hand touched him. That is why he says, 'The Lord stretched out his hand toward me and touched my mouth, and the Lord said to me, Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot.' (Jeremiah 1:9-10)
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet is touched by the Lord's own hand.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words of God first uproot and pull down the bad things and afterwards build and plant, because God cannot build on the place of the bad building.
comments.comment:
But the words of God do not stop at 'to uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' (Jeremiah 1:10) Suppose the bad things have been uprooted from me, the worse things pulled down: what good is it to me if, in place of what was uprooted, the better things are not planted? What good is it to me if, in place of these, the things that matter are not built up? That is why the words of God first, of necessity, do the 'uproot and pull down and destroy,' (Jeremiah 1:10) and after that the 'build and plant.' And we have always watched in Scripture that the things which look grim, if I may call them so, are named first, then the things that seem cheerful are said second. 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) He did not say, 'I will make alive,' and after that, 'I will kill.' For it is impossible that what God has made alive should be taken away by him or by anyone else. But 'I will kill and I will make alive.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) Whom will I kill? Paul the betrayer, Paul the persecutor. 'And I will make alive,' (Deuteronomy 32:39) so that he may become 'Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ.' (1 Corinthians 1:1)

If the wretched people from the heresies had understood these things, they would not keep putting them forward to us, saying, Do you see how fierce and inhuman the God of the Law is, when he says, 'I will kill, and I will make alive'? Do you not see in the Scriptures a promise of the resurrection of the dead? Or do you not see the resurrection of the dead already making its beginning in each person? 'We were buried' with Christ 'through baptism' and we were raised with him.

So he begins from the grimmer voices, which are necessary — as 'I will kill' — then, having killed, 'and I will make alive. I will strike, and I will heal.' (Deuteronomy 32:39) 'For whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives.' (Hebrews 12:6) First he strikes, and after that he heals. 'For he makes one feel pain and again restores.' (Hebrews 12:6) So also here: 'I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and to pull down and to destroy and to build and to plant.' (Jeremiah 1:10) Only, first those bad things must be taken from us. God cannot build on the place of the bad building. 'For what partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? What fellowship has light with darkness?' (2 Corinthians 6:14) Vice must be uprooted from the foundations. The building of vice must be consumed from our soul, so that after these things the words of God may build and plant.

I cannot understand what is written in any other way: 'Behold, I have given my words into your mouth.' (Jeremiah 1:9) What do the words do? 'To uproot and to pull down and to destroy.' (Jeremiah 1:10) Words uproot 'nations'; words pull down kingdoms — not these worldly ones. Think, in a way worthy of words that pull down, worthy of words that uproot, the things uprooted by words, the things pulled down by words. Is there not, in what is being said right now, a power — if God gives it (according to 'the Lord will give a word to those who preach good news with great power' (Psalm 68:11)) — a power that uproots, if there is any unbelief, any hypocrisy, any vice, any incontinence? Is there not a power that pulls down, if somewhere an idol-shrine has been built in the heart, so that when that is pulled down a temple of God may be built, and the glory of God may be found in the temple built up, and there may be not a grove but a planting, a garden of God, where the temple of God is, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse puts uprooting before building and planting.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The nations and kingdoms that the words uproot are the sins in the soul, which the heavenly Father did not plant, so Jeremiah's gift is not a grim one.
comments.comment:
Who is so blessed as to uproot, by the words given by God, the many kingdoms which 'the devil shows,' kingdoms of opposing powers, kingdoms according to the sins? For it is written, 'Behold, I have given my words into your mouth. Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot.' (Jeremiah 1:10) And as there are kingdoms, so there are nations. A kingdom cannot even be called a kingdom unless it has nations under it. For example: there is a kingdom of fornication, and the nations of fornication are each several fornication. There is one kingdom, the general sin of greed and of robbery, and there are many kingdoms in those who have many kinds of sins. Then, in each of the sinners, think of the nations under the kingdom: this man has many nations of the kingdom according to fornication, that man has many nations of the kingdom according to robbery, according to slander, according to anger.

It is the work of the words of God, sent out over 'nations and kingdoms,' (Jeremiah 1:10) 'to uproot and to pull down.' (Jeremiah 1:10) To uproot what? The Savior taught, saying, 'Every plant which my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted.' (Matthew 15:13) There are some things inside in the souls which 'the heavenly Father did not plant.' For all 'the evil reasonings, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witnesses, blasphemies' (Matthew 15:19) are plants planted not by the heavenly Father. And if you want to see whose plants such reasonings are, hear that 'an enemy man did this,' the one who sowed 'the tares in the midst of the wheat.' (Matthew 13:25) So God stands by, having the seeds, and the devil. If we give 'place to the devil,' 'the enemy' sows a plant 'which the Father did not plant,' which will certainly be uprooted. If we do not give 'place to the devil,' but give place to God, God rejoices and sows his seeds on our governing mind.

Do not think, then, that Jeremiah received some grim gift from God, because he is set 'over nations and over kingdoms, to uproot.' (Jeremiah 1:10) God is good, uprooting through the words the bad things, the kingdoms hostile to the kingdom of the heavens, the warring nations against the nation of God. 'To uproot and to pull down.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The nations and kingdoms that the words of God uproot are to be taken as a figure of the bad things in the souls of men.
comments.comment: Everyone who has received words from God and has the grace of the heavenly words has received them in order 'to uproot nations and kingdoms and to pull them down.' (Jeremiah 1:10) But if it is said that everyone who has received words from God 'uproots nations and kingdoms,' do not take the nations and the kingdoms for me in a bodily way. Look at human souls, ruled by sin, as the apostle said: 'Do not let sin reign in our mortal body.' (Romans 6:12) And seeing the many kinds of sins, take the nations and the kingdoms as a figure: the bad things in the souls of men, which are uprooted and pulled down by the words of God given either to Jeremiah or to anyone at all.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what "nations and kingdoms" to be uprooted means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The almond staff Jeremiah saw, with God's reply that he is keeping watch, fits the almond rod as a symbol of sleeplessness and so of Christ's awakening from death.
comments.comment: [On Aaron's almond rod:] a rod of almond wood is not without power to cause sleeplessness if it is laid near a person’s head, perhaps producing this effect through natural powers, by the will of God. And he who knows all things, the Maker of the universe, will in some way confirm this for us himself when he says to Jeremiah: ‘What do you see, Jeremiah?’ And Jeremiah said, ‘A staff of almond wood.’ To this God says: ‘You have seen rightly, for I am keeping watch over my words, to perform them’ (Jeremiah 1:11–12). The almond rod, then, would fittingly be understood as a symbol of sleeplessness. And Christ’s return to life from the dead was an awakening, as if from sleep. That is why he also says through the lyre of the Psalmist: ‘I lay down and slept; I awoke, for the Lord upheld me’ (Psalm 3:5).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 10

comments.capsule: One who is beginning in the virtue of mercy and being led toward perfection in love can say that the truth of Christ is in him.
comments.comment: And in Jeremiah, he who is beginning in the virtue of mercy, it is necessary, as the one speaking of God says to the God-fearing: 'Remember the mercy of your youth and the perfection of your love' (Jeremiah 2:2); for he who is beginning in mercy, as also he who is led toward perfection in love, is able to say, 'There is the truth of Christ in me.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The flock is harmed because its leaders fell into ungodliness and went after useless things.
comments.comment: Indeed, harm has surpassed the flock because of the leaders who fell into ungodliness, about whom God Himself says: "The shepherds were unfaithful to me, and behind useless things they went" (Jeremiah 2:8), as they attend to both divination and false dreams being promised, just as the sheep themselves are being harmed, undergoing destruction. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Heaven is astonished that Israel left God for crushed cisterns, since from the order of creation they could have understood its Maker.
comments.comment: [Of God, speaking in Jeremiah:] And as it were astonished at the undiluted unlearnings of those from Israel, he says somehow thus: ‘Heaven was astonished upon this, and the earth shuddered still more very much, says the Lord; because my people did two evil things. Me they left—a spring of living water—and they dug for themselves crushed cisterns, which will not be able to hold water.’ (Jeremiah 2:12–13) For I would think, and very reasonably, that those standing off from the worship unto God, serving the creation beside the Creator and Maker, or still leaping down toward a more shameful wandering, worshiping the works of their own hands, miss every good-counsel; although it was easy, if indeed they should choose to think rightly, to look down upon the beauty of the nature above all and unspeakable from the creation of a world, and from the good-order of the things come to be to understand the orderer and leader and craftsman of this all.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 6

comments.capsule: The prophet calls God a fountain and the Holy Spirit living water, which cleanses our sins in baptism.
comments.comment: Jeremiah, in the person of God, says: 'The heavens were out of joint at this, and the earth trembled at this: because my people have done two evil things. They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have hewn for themselves broken cisterns, which cannot hold water' (Jeremiah 2:12). The prophet mystically sets forth the mystery. For he called God 'a fountain' and called the holy Spirit 'living water,' who in the baptismal pool cleanses all our sins, being unable to be split apart by the nature of the intellectual fountain, just as a stream from fountains cannot.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who abandon the fountain of living water and promise life-giving water do not wash people but make them filthy and heap up their sins.
comments.comment: [Of those who have left the church and baptize:] The Lord points these same people out again and marks them, saying: "They have abandoned me, the fountain of living water, and dug for themselves worn-out cisterns that cannot hold water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Since there can be no baptism other than the one, they suppose they can baptize. With the fountain of life abandoned, they promise the grace of life-giving and saving water. People are not washed there but rather made filthy, nor are their sins cleansed but instead heaped up. That birth produces children not for God but for the devil.
comments.author: Cyprian of Carthage
comments.work: On the Unity of the Catholic Church

comments.capsule: God did not make death or evil, and the prophet asks in reproof how the vine God planted all true turned into bitterness.
comments.comment:
'God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living. For he created all things that they might be, and the generations of the world are saving, and there is no poison of ruin in them, nor a kingdom of Hades upon the earth.' (Wisdom of Solomon 1:13–14) Then, going a little past the wording, I will say from where death entered: 'By the envy of the devil death entered into the world.' (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24) So whatever is best about us, God has made; but we have created evil and sins for ourselves.

That is why here too the beginning of the reading in the prophet was speaking, as it were questioningly, to those who have had bitterness in the soul, opposite to the sweetness which God prepared for it: 'How have you turned into bitterness, the alien vine?' (Jeremiah 2:21) As if he were saying: God did not make lameness, but he made all sound of foot — what then has become the cause of those who have been lamed? And God made all the members healthy in the first place — what has become a cause of someone suffering something? …

So here the Word is at a loss toward those who sin, speaking as a reproof: 'How have you turned into bitterness, the alien vine? For I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, all true.' In what was said before this it has been spoken, and taking up a little I will persuade you that God planted a good vine, the soul of man, and each, having turned, has become opposite to the will of the one who created him. 'And I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, all' — not in part — 'true,' not one true and one false, but 'I planted you a fruit-bearing vine, all true. How have you turned' — I planted you an all-true vine; you, how have you turned into bitterness and become an alien vine?
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet asks how the true vine turned bitter.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nitre and soap, as words that cleanse, can wash some sins, but there are sins that need the spirit of burning and not nitre or soap.
comments.comment:
After this let us look at: 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained in your injustices before me, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 2:22) Did some sinning soul suppose that, taking nitre and washing with ordinary nitre, it ceases from the stain and ceases from the sin? Did someone assume that, taking this herb that springs from the earth and washing and scouring, the soul is cleansed, because the Word says here to the one who has turned into bitterness and become an alien vine, 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained in your injustices before me, says the Lord' (Jeremiah 2:22)?

But one must know that the Word has all power. And as he has the power of all Scripture, so the Word has the power of every medicine, and is the power of everything that cleanses, and is most scouring. 'For the word of God is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword.' (Hebrews 4:12) And whatever you name, of which there is need, that is in the power of the Word. So there is a word that is nitre, and there is a word that is soap, which, when spoken, cleanses such filth. But since not every sin is healed from such a word as is nitre, and from such a word as is soap — there are sins that do not need nitre or soap — it is said to the one who thinks it has sins of a kind that can be washed off in nitre and soap: 'If you wash yourself with nitre and multiply soap for yourself, you are stained before me in your injustices, says the Lord.' (Isaiah 4:4)

And as of wounds some are healed with a poultice, and others with oil, and others need a bandage and so are made well, and there are other wounds of which it is said, 'There is no poultice to put on, nor oil nor bandages; but your land is desolate, your cities burned with fire' (Isaiah 1:7) — so there are some sins which soil the soul, and for these sins the man needs a word that is nitre, a word that is soap. And there are some sins which are not healed this way, for they are not even compared to soil. That is why the Lord in Isaiah, knowing the differences of sins, see how he says, 'The Lord will wash the soil of the sons and of the daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst with a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.' Soil and blood: soil with a spirit of judgment, blood with a spirit of burning. If you have sinned, yet not 'unto death,' you have been soiled. So 'the Lord will wash the soil of the sons and of the daughters of Zion, and he will cleanse the blood from their midst.' (Isaiah 4:4) Then the matching: toward 'the soil,' 'with a spirit of judgment'; toward 'the blood,' 'with a spirit of burning.' And most of us, if we have sinned the worse things, do not need nitre, nor the multiplying of soap, but the spirit of burning.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of washing with nitre and soap.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord says he did not become a wilderness or untilled land to Israel, so the hearer must search out what is meant.
comments.comment:
The Lord says at the start of what was read about Israel, that he did not become a wilderness to him, nor untilled land. Who, standing in the place of these words, would not search out what is meant?

Grant that God did not become a wilderness in Israel, and did not become untilled land in Israel. Has the Lord then become a wilderness to Israel today, or is he untilled land to them now? And when he was not a wilderness to Israel, nor untilled land, was he a wilderness and untilled land to the nations?

If he is never a wilderness to anyone, and never untilled land to anyone, what need was there to say it to Israel in particular: 'Did I become a wilderness to the house of Israel, or untilled land?' (Jeremiah 2:31) We may come first to the common benefits of God, and after those, to the ones that belong to a people.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is a wilderness to no one in the common account, he was none to Israel when he did wonders, and when he turned from Israel grace was poured out on the nations.
comments.comment:
God is a wilderness to no one, making the sun rise on the evil and on the good; he is untilled land to no one, sending rain on the just and on the unjust. How is he a wilderness, who makes day and night for rest? How is he a wilderness, who makes the earth bear fruit? How is he a wilderness, who orders each soul so that it may be rational, take up knowledge, train its understanding, and have its senses sound? So as to the common account, God is a wilderness to no one.

As to the particular, I come to Israel's affairs and I say: he was neither wilderness nor untilled land when he did the signs and wonders for the people in Egypt. If a time came when they were abandoned, he became, as it were, a wilderness to them, though he himself was not a wilderness.

When he was not a wilderness to Israel, nor untilled land, he was, on the particular account, a wilderness and untilled land to the nations. But when he turned away from Israel, and became to that Israel a wilderness and untilled land, then grace was poured out on the nations, and now Christ Jesus has become to us not a wilderness but full, not untilled land but fruit-bearing. For 'the children of the desolate are more than of her who has a husband.' (Isaiah 54:1)

And he threatens those to whom he was not a wilderness nor untilled land, saying: I did not become a wilderness to you, nor untilled land, but you have said, 'We will not be ruled; we will not come to you any more.' (Jeremiah 2:31) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God was not a wilderness to Israel.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Synagogue played the harlot with many shepherds by following the commandments of men and disregarding the spiritual Bridegroom, and turning from what is right to attach oneself to unholy teachers is spiritual harlotry.
comments.comment: The passage [the law on a priest's household] also seems to hint at the misfortune of the Synagogue of the Jews. Because she played the harlot with many shepherds, as it is written (Jeremiah 3:1), Christ did not receive her into spiritual fellowship … He made the mystery plainer still when he said: ‘And if the daughter of a priest profanes herself by playing the harlot, she profanes the name of her father; she shall be burned with fire.’ (Leviticus 21:9) For the Synagogue of the Jews has been given over to the flame as unholy and profane, because she followed the opinions of the scribes and Pharisees and devoted her whole mind to the commandments of men (Matthew 15:9). So it was very just that she heard the prophet say: ‘How have you become a harlot, faithful city of Zion, full of justice?’ (Isaiah 1:21) Having played the harlot, then, and utterly disregarded the spiritual Bridegroom from above, she has become fuel for the fire. … To turn away from what is right, then, and to seek to attach oneself to shameful and unholy teachers, is a form of spiritual harlotry.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The high mountain stands for boasting and high-mindedness, as in the Pharisee in the temple, and the grove-tree for words that bear no fruit, which is why the law forbids planting a grove beside the altar.
comments.comment:
And he speaks to us through the prophets and says: 'Have you seen what the dwelling of Israel has done to me?' (Jeremiah 3:6) Understand that Israel as that people. 'She went upon every high mountain and under every shady tree.' (Jeremiah 3:6)

If you see the Pharisee going up into the temple boastfully, not striking his own breast, not caring for his own evils, but saying, 'I thank you that I am not as the rest of men, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this tax-collector; I fast twice in the sabbath, I tithe what I have,' (Luke 18:11–12) you will see that he has gone up 'upon every high mountain' in a blameworthy way, and having loved high-mindedness, and according to boast and according to pride every high hill, and has come to be 'under every tree' not fruit-bearing, but 'of a grove.' For a grove-tree is one thing, and a tree planted into groves is another: when they plant trees, they do not plant the fruit-bearing ones, not a fig, not a vine, but only, for pleasure, trees without fruit. You will find the words of the heterodox like that, and the beauties of their persuasions, not turning those who hear.

When then someone gives himself to such words, he has gone 'under every grove-tree.' He did not say 'every tree' and stop, nor again add 'every fruit-bearing tree,' but said 'under every grove-tree.' For this reason you will understand why the lawgiver says: 'You shall not plant any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God, and you shall not make a grove.' (Deuteronomy 16:21) For you have the name of the grove itself forbidden.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'every high mountain and every grove-tree' through a Gospel picture a reader knows.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel took over the mountain peaks and the groves, built altars there and sacrificed to unclean demons, and some did not spare even their own children.
comments.comment: The God of all makes this plain through the voice of Jeremiah, saying: “Have you seen what the house of Israel has done to me? They went up on every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and there they prostituted themselves” (Jeremiah 3:6). For they took over the mountain peaks and the most flowering parts of the groves, built altars and sacred precincts, and brought sacrifices and drink offerings there to the unclean demons. And there were some who did not spare even their own children. Jechonias, indeed, slaughtered his own son to gods that do not exist.
comments.selected_reason: Says concretely what the high mountains and leafy trees were.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What happened to Israel is written as a warning to us, for if God did not spare the natural branches he will not spare us, and he is both kind and severe because we need both.
comments.comment:
If then he says, as it were: first I sent Israel away because of the sins, and I sent him into a removal, and Judah, hearing what had happened to Israel, did not turn — he is speaking about our sins.

The things that happened to Israel are read, and the falls concerning that people. We ought to fear: 'if he did not spare the natural branches, how much more not you?' (Romans 11:21–22) If, not sparing those who boast to be a cultivated olive, those rooted into the root of the patriarchs Abraham and Isaac and Jacob, the God who is kind and also a lover of man cut them out, how much more will he not spare us?

For he is not kind and not severe, nor severe and not kind. If he were only kind, and not severe, we would have despised his kindness still more. If he were severe, and not kind, perhaps we would even have despaired over our sins. But now, as God — for we who repent need his kindness, and we who remain in sins need his severity — God is both kind and severe.
comments.selected_reason: Draws a plain lesson from Israel's fall and explains why God is both kind and severe.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Israel, the northern kingdom, sinned first and was carried captive to Assyria, and Judah, hearing of its falls, sinned still more, until the sins of Israel compared with Judah's seemed like righteousness.
comments.comment:
He wants us to know that, as it is written in the Books of Kingdoms, the people was divided in the days of Rehoboam into the kingdom of the ten tribes under Jeroboam and the kingdom of two tribes under Rehoboam. Those under Jeroboam were called Israel, and those under Rehoboam Judah. This division of the people has remained, as far as the history goes, until now. We do not know a history that has gathered Israel and Judah into one.

Israel sinned first, and more — the Israel under Jeroboam and his successors — and sinned so far beyond Judah that they were condemned by providence to become captives to the Assyrians, as the Scripture says, 'until this day.' After that the sons of Judah also sinned, and were condemned as captives to Babylon, not 'until this day' as Israel was, but for seventy years, of which Jeremiah prophesied, and of which Daniel also made mention.

If we take these things of that people then, look at the prophet's words and see whether they do not show something of this kind. He accuses the sins of Israel, and says that when so many sins had come to be for Israel, the congregation of Judah heard their falls, and in what way he had made them captives, and was not trained by it, but added to the sins, so that by the addition, when the sins were compared with the sins of Israel, righteousness was found in Israel rather than in Judah.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those born of Abraham lost the covenant and were not helped by being from the fathers, so we who sin shall be abandoned all the more.
comments.comment: We too have been reproached — I mean we who sin and do not keep the covenants of God, and do not see that those others, well-born, from Abraham, having received a promise, have lost the covenant. We ought then to reckon that they have fallen from the blessings and the promises, and that being from the fathers did them no good — how much more shall we, if we sin, be abandoned. 'If you were children of Abraham, you would do the works of Abraham,' (John 8:39) the Savior says to them. And again John: 'Do not begin to say in yourselves, We have Abraham as father; for I say to you that God is able from these stones to raise children to Abraham' (Matthew 3:9) — hinting at us, who have a heart of stone and are hardened toward the truth. And truly God has raised children to Abraham from the stones, if we remain in the bringing-forth of children and keep the spirit of adoption.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A newly bought servant learns whom the master honored and whom he threw out and imitates the first, and so we should read Scripture, imitate those justified and guard against the falls of those thrown out.
comments.comment: Someone entered the house of a master of a house. He is newly bought. He asks whom of the former household servants the master honored and why, whom he dishonored and why. Having understood, if he wants to remain in the house of the master, he guards himself from falling into what the former slaves did who sinned and were thrown out and given over to punishment. Then, having learned what the former slaves did who were well-pleasing, and upon what sort of things they obtained freedom, he imitates those. We too were not slaves of God, but of idols and demons, Gentiles; yesterday and the day before we came to God. Let us read the Scripture, see who was justified, who was condemned; let us imitate those justified, and guard ourselves from falling into the things into which those taken captive fell, those thrown out from God.
comments.selected_reason: A simple picture of why Judah should have learned from Israel and why we should learn from Scripture.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As a husband under Moses' law sends away a wife with a bill of divorce, God sent Israel away, and the lack of prophets, signs, temple and sacrifices among them shows they received it.
comments.comment:
If you understand these two peoples, the one from Israel and the one from the nations, see with me the removal of Israel also upon that people of Israel, and understand it written about them: 'I have sent her away and given her a bill of divorce.' (Jeremiah 3:8) For God sent that people away and gave it a bill of divorce.

It is like those who have married: if the wife is displeasing to the husband, the law of Moses says a bill of divorce came from the husband and the wife was sent away, and it was permitted to the one who sent the first wife away, because she seemed to have acted unseemly, to marry another. In the same way, by the Word, see those receiving a bill of divorce. And because they received the bill of divorce, they were abandoned altogether. Where are prophets still among them? Where signs still among them? Where an appearing of God? Where the worship, the temple, the sacrifices? They have been thrown out from their own place. So he gave Israel a bill of divorce.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the bill of divorce by the law of marriage and what Israel lost.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judah ought to have been trained by what Israel suffered, but instead added to its sins, so that Israel's sins seem righteousness beside them.
comments.comment: After so many things that I did to Israel, sending him away, giving a bill of divorce, the congregation of Judah ought to have been trained by what those others suffered. They were not only not trained, but they added to the sins, so that the sins of the congregation of Israel, compared with the sins of the congregation of Judah, seem to be righteousness.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judah followed Israel into harlotry, and when we sin we do the same, committing adultery with the stone and with the wood.
comments.comment: 'And faithless Judah was not afraid, and she went and played the harlot also.' (Jeremiah 3:8–10) Israel having played the harlot first, Judah later played the harlot too. 'And her harlotry came to nothing, and she committed adultery with the wood and the stone.' (Jeremiah 3:9) When we sin, we do nothing else than, becoming stone-hearted, commit adultery with the stone. When we sin and play the harlot 'under every grove-tree,' we too commit adultery with the wood.
comments.selected_reason: Applies the verse's picture of adultery with wood and stone to the reader's own sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Turning to God deficiently is not turning with the whole heart, and true turning is to learn from those justified and those blamed in Scripture and write it into the heart, so that no bill of divorce is given to us.
comments.comment:
'And faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in a lie.' (Jeremiah 3:10) If we have turned to God, but deficiently, we are accused as not having turned 'with the whole heart.' Therefore 'faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart.' He did not say: and faithless Judah turned, and she stood; but: 'and faithless Judah did not turn to me with her whole heart, but in a lie' she turned.

True turning, then, is to read the old things, to know those who were justified, to imitate them; to read those things, to see those who were blamed, to guard ourselves from falling into those blames; to read the books of the new covenant, the words of the apostles; after reading, to write all these things into the heart, to live according to them, so that a bill of divorce may not be given to us also, but that we may be able to come to the holy inheritance, and that, the fullness of the nations having been saved, Israel may then be able to enter.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what turning 'with the whole heart' means in practice.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Judah turned in a lie, not in truth, and so Israel's sins beside Judah's became a justification of Israel's soul.
comments.comment: She was not ashamed before me of what I had done to Israel, that she might turn completely. She ought to have turned in truth, and she turned in a lie. And the Lord said to me: 'Israel has justified her soul from faithless Judah.' The sins of Israel, compared with the falls of Judah, have become a justification of the soul of the congregation of Israel.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's surprising saying that Israel is more righteous than Judah.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The call of the nations began from the fall of Israel, for the many sins of that people left it abandoned and brought us, who were strangers to the covenants, to the hope of the promise.
comments.comment:
'Go, then, and read these words toward the north.' (Jeremiah 3:12) If the wording has been understood, let us see what he wants to be shown in these things.

The call of the nations had its beginning from the fall of Israel. And the apostles, preaching to the synagogues of the Jews, say: 'To you the word of salvation was sent; since you judge yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the nations.' (Acts 13:46) And the apostle, knowing what he knows about these things, says: 'By their fall salvation has come to the nations, to make them jealous.' (Romans 11:11)

So the many sins of that people made it to be abandoned, and made us come to the hope of the promise, we who were strangers to the covenants.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God promises his flocks shepherds according to his heart who shepherd with knowledge, and perhaps these are the apostles, prophets, teachers and evangelists who wisely instruct the assembly of Christ.
comments.comment: Concerning those who excellently perform the oversight they were handed, it is said by God: 'I will give to them'—clearly to the flocks—'shepherds according to my heart, and they shall shepherd them, shepherding with knowledge' (Jer 3:15). Concerning those who thus shepherd the flock with knowledge, the Christ-bearing Apostle remembers those placed in the Church with the apostles and prophets, as teachers and evangelists. And perhaps apostles and prophets, teachers and evangelists, are those who gnostically and prudently instruct the assembly of Christ …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If our tilling is bad, shame consumes the labors of the fathers, but if it is good the firstborn are offered to God, and the soul's offspring are thoughts as sons and works as daughters.
comments.comment:
'Shame,' then, 'has consumed the labors of our fathers from their youth—their sheep and their oxen.' (Jeremiah 3:24; 8:17) What is there in us that is tilling us—whether tilling badly (so that 'badly' is said of the tiller) or tilling well? If it tills badly, that is labor of the fathers being consumed by their shame. If it tills well, it is not the fathers' labor, but labor from which the firstborn are offered upon God's altar. They say 'their sons and their daughters.' (Wisdom of Solomon 7:27; cf. John 1:12–13; Romans 8:14–16) Whose 'their'? Are the sons of 'them' or of 'the fathers' consumed by their shame? And we have often said that the offspring of the soul are these: thoughts are sons, and the works and bodily practices are daughters.

Since there are wicked thoughts—such as those from the nations thought—and wicked works as well, sons and daughters are consumed by those who made them, if shame arises in them over what was sinned. May it not be that we make sons and daughters for a consumption that comes from shame.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'We have sinned' belongs to one who sinned before and has carefully repented, not to one who is still sinning, and turning takes time, as healing does for wounds.
comments.comment:
'For we have sinned against our God, we and our fathers.' (Daniel 9:5 (LXX)) Would that we also would say it as these do, according to the prophet's personification.

'We have sinned.' 'We have sinned' is not the same as 'we are sinning.' The one still in sin should not say 'we have sinned'; the one who sinned before and has carefully repented should say 'we have sinned'—as also in Daniel there is written the confession of those no longer sinning: 'We have sinned, we have acted lawlessly,' (Psalm 25:7 (LXX)) and in the Psalms: 'Do not remember our ancient lawless deeds,' (Jeremiah 3:25 (LXX)) the prophet says. So let us also confess our sins—would that they were not yesterday's, would that they were not three days old, but would that in confessing we confess sins done fifteen years ago, by having no sin after those for fifteen years. But if we sinned yesterday, we are not yet trustworthy when we confess our sins; nor is there yet room for these sins of ours to be wiped away. 'For we have sinned, we and our fathers, from our youth until this day.'

Let that stand otherwise as teaching about the best manner of confession. These words are an accusation of long sinning. 'From youth,' it says, 'until this day, and we have not obeyed the voice of the Lord our God.' We have sinned, and we have not obeyed until the present. Then, turning and having a beginning of turning, they say, 'We have sinned, and we have not obeyed.' For not at the same moment of wanting to obey do we already obey at once. Time is still needed, as with wounds toward healing, so also with turning—toward turning completely and purely to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the right way to confess sins in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God requires a complete turning, with the abominations of slander and idle words removed from the mouth and awe that comes from knowing the face of God.
comments.comment:
Upon these things God says concerning Israel: 'If Israel turns to me, says the Lord, he will also turn'—that is, if he turns completely, he will turn with a turning, not if he merely begins, as it were, to turn. Then he says: 'And if he removes his abominations from his mouth, and stands in awe before my face, and swears, “As the Lord lives,” in truth and in judgment and in righteousness, then nations will bless themselves in him.'

If they do these things, 'nations will bless themselves in him.' (Jeremiah 4:2) What must they do so that nations bless themselves in him? 'If he removes his abominations from his mouth.' (Jeremiah 4:1) What is removing abominations from the mouth? Whatever we speak badly are abominations in our mouth. So let us remove the abominations from our mouth, taking away slanders, empty words, idle words that will make us answerable on the day of judgment—'for by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.' (Matthew 12:37)

Next is also, 'You will stand in awe before my face.' Let us do this second thing, not simply so that we may be reverent. For there can be a reverence that does not come from the face of God. Those who fear without knowledge, though they propose to fear, do not stand in awe from the face of God. But as many as stand in awe with knowledge—by always looking and painting for themselves the face of God that comes upon those who do evil, to wipe out their memory from the earth—these are the ones who stand in awe from the face of God.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what removing abominations from the mouth and standing in awe mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: An oath must be made in truth, in judgment and in righteousness, and a true oath sworn by habit without judgment is still not well made.
comments.comment:
'If he removes his abominations from his mouth, and stands in awe before my face, and swears: “As the Lord lives,” (Jeremiah 4:1–2) in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.'

Let us look at ourselves who swear—how we do not swear in judgment but without judgment, so that our oaths come by habit rather than by judgment. We are carried away, and the word, exposing this, says: 'And if he swears, “As the Lord lives,” (Jeremiah 4:2) in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.' We know what the Lord said to the disciples in the Gospel: 'But I say to you, do not swear at all.' Let us look at this saying too; and if God grants, both will be examined together. Perhaps one must first swear 'in truth and in judgment and in righteousness.'

In the one who swears I first look for what is not false but true, so that he may swear with truth. Yet we wretched ones even swear falsely. But even if it is 'with truth,' an oath is still not well made unless it is also 'in judgment.' For grant that I swear by habit—I do not swear 'in judgment.' If one must take for such an oath the God of all and his Christ upon this matter, how great must the matter be before I bend the knee and swear? Perhaps I would do it sometime to heal unbelief that has arisen in some about my word.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the three conditions of the oath in the verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Break new ground' is said especially to teachers, who must make new ground in the souls of their hearers before sowing the holy seeds, so that they do not sow among thorns.
comments.comment:
So 'thus says the Lord to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem: Break new ground for yourselves, and do not sow among thorns.' (Jeremiah 4:3) This word is spoken especially to those who teach, so that they not entrust what is said to the hearers before they make new ground in their souls. For when, putting hand to the plow, they make new ground in souls—according to the good and fine soil of those who hear—then as they sow they do not sow among thorns.

But if, before the plow and before making new ground in the ruling principle of the hearers, someone takes the holy seeds—the word about the Father, about the Son, about the Holy Spirit, about resurrection, about punishment, about rest, about law, about prophets, and in short about each of the things written—and sows them, he transgresses the command that says first, 'Break new ground for yourselves,' and second, 'Do not sow among thorns.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what making new ground and sowing among thorns mean for teaching.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Every hearer must become a farmer of himself, finding the thorns in his soul and plowing it new with the rational plow before he takes seed from teachers.
comments.comment: But one of the hearers will say: 'I do not teach; I am not under this command.' You too become a farmer of yourself, and do not sow among thorns, but make new ground for me in the plot God of all has entrusted to you. Consider the plot; see where the thorns are—where cares of life and deceit of wealth and love of pleasure are. Having seen the thorns in your soul, seek the rational plow about which Jesus says, 'No one who puts hand to the plow and turns back is fit for the kingdom of God.' Having sought it and found it, gathering from the Scriptures the pure working oxen, plow and renew the land, and so that it may no longer be old, make it new—putting off the old man with his practices and putting on the new man renewed into knowledge.
comments.selected_reason: Applies the verse to every reader, not only to teachers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Once the ground is new, seeds are taken from the law, the prophets, the Gospels and the apostles and sown through memory and study, and God, not the seed, makes them grow.
comments.comment: You will make new ground for yourself, and if you make the new ground, take seeds from those who teach, take seeds from the law, from the prophets, from the Gospel writings, from the apostolic words, and having taken these seeds sow the soul through memory and study. They will seem to spring up of themselves; but in truth after the memory of them it is not they that spring up, but God who grows them: 'I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.' (1 Corinthians 3:6) And if anyone has been able to understand the Scriptures, that one has made new ground, and having made it has sown not among thorns. These seeds are managed by God not to become an ear all at once, but as in the Gospel according to Mark: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Circumcision counts only when it is 'to your God': the priests of Egyptian idols are circumcised too, but to idols, while one in communion with the church's rule is circumcised to God, and the heart has a foreskin to be removed.
comments.comment:
And next to this it is said: 'Be circumcised to your God; circumcise the foreskin of your heart.' (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jer 4:4) 'Be circumcised to your God'—necessarily is added 'to your God.' You will understand it from the sensible example. According to the sensible I say: not only those of the circumcision according to Moses' law are circumcised, but many others also. The priests of the Egyptians' idols are circumcised, but that circumcision is circumcision to idols and is not circumcision done to God. The Jews' circumcision, perhaps—and certainly then—was done to God.

So when the word says, 'Be circumcised to your God,' understand the saying and move also to the figurative reading, so that you find how, among figurative circumcisions (so that some of them might even say, 'We are the circumcision'), some are circumcised to God, and others are circumcised, yet not to God. There are also other words besides the word of truth, besides the word of the church. Those who philosophize chastise manners and the heart, and those from the heresies chastise, and circumcision happens for them. But it is circumcision, yet not to God; for circumcision happens among them by a false word.

But when according to the church's rule, according to the aim of sound teaching, you are in communion, you are not only circumcised—you are circumcised 'to God.' So 'Be circumcised to your God, and circumcise the foreskin of your heart.' (Jeremiah 4:4) Who does not pass these words by as clear? So there is a foreskin of the heart, and this must be circumcised.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says 'to your God' and what a foreskin of the heart is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The foreskin is born with us and circumcision removes what comes from birth, so the command to circumcise the heart implies something born with the heart that must be removed.
comments.comment: The one who works the word carefully, searching such things in this place, will examine: foreskin is born with us; circumcision is acquired; and what has come from birth, circumcision removes. If then the word commands the foreskin of the heart to be removed, there must be something born with the heart which he calls foreskin, which must be removed so that someone may be circumcised as to the foreskin of the heart. If anyone understands, 'We were by nature children of wrath, like the rest' (Ephesians 2:3; Prov 20:9); if anyone understands 'the body of our humiliation' in which we were born; if anyone understands, 'No one is clean from filth, not even if his life is one day; his months are numbered'—he will see how we were born with uncleanness and with the foreskin of our heart.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: False opinions arise in the soul in its first age, and the word that cleanses doctrines and removes them takes away the foreskin of the heart.
comments.comment: So that it may be said according to a simpler example able to lead you to see 'the foreskin of the heart,' I will set beside this that in the first age false opinions certainly arise in the soul. For it is not possible for a human being from the beginning to take true doctrines. … the foreskin of the heart comes before circumcision. So we need to take the word that cleanses the doctrines and removes everything that has come to be in us according to false opinion. This, then, is putting away the foreskin of our heart. For if the heart is, for us, what has the ruling principle—where the thoughts are, from which the reasonings go out—the one who removes evil reasonings removes 'the foreskin of the heart'; the one who puts away false opinion is circumcised as to the foreskin of his heart and becomes a man of Judah and one dwelling in Jerusalem, being circumcised.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a simple meaning for the foreskin of the heart: false opinion removed by the word.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Lord's wrath goes out like fire against those who have not put away the foreskin of the heart, and the wickedness of our practices is the matter that fire feeds on.
comments.comment: But if someone does not put away the foreskin of his heart, let us see what the word threatens him: 'Lest my wrath go out,' it says, 'like fire and be kindled, and there will be none to quench it.' (Deuteronomy 10:16; Jer 4:4; Rom 2:29) So the wrath of the Lord goes out like fire upon those not circumcised to God, upon those who have not put away the foreskin of their heart, 'and there will be none to quench it from before the wickedness of their practices.' (Jeremiah 4:4) That fire has as its matter the wickedness of our practices. Where there is no wickedness of practices, the fire has nowhere to spread.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the threat of unquenchable fire in the verse.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The visible Judah and Jerusalem are the land and the synagogue, the spiritual ones are the Church of those circumcised in the Spirit, and Paul knows a Jew inwardly whose circumcision is of the heart.
comments.comment: By the visible Judah, and Jerusalem too, we mean the land itself in which Israel dwelt, and the very body of the synagogue of the Jews. The spiritual Jerusalem, or Judah, we hold to be the Church, that is, the circumcision in the Spirit: those who have the circumcision made without hands in Christ (Colossians 2:11) in mind and heart. So one of the holy prophets cried out to the Jews: “Be circumcised to God, and circumcise your hardness of heart, men of Judah and you who dwell in Jerusalem” (Jeremiah 4:4). And the divine Paul knows another Jew, not the one according to the flesh but the one in the spirit, for he writes: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter; his praise is not from men but from God” (Romans 2:28–29).
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The spiritual circumcision of one who has God is of the heart and not of the flesh, as the prophet tells those striving only according to the flesh.
comments.comment: It must be considered what the spiritual circumcision is, which one having God is circumcised, not necessarily one being circumcised according to the flesh. For the prophet says to those striving only according to the flesh: 'Be circumcised to your God, and do not circumcise the flesh of your uncircumcision' (Jeremiah 4:4); and the same prophet says: 'All Gentiles are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts' (Jeremiah 9:26). Therefore, he who is sensibly circumcised removes something of that which serves the generation of the member, just as he who casting out every thought friendly to the generation of the intellect circumcises the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The trumpet is the lofty word that wakes the hearer for the fight against the passions.
comments.comment: 'Signal with a trumpet upon the earth.' (Jeremiah 4:5) The lofty word—the one that wakes the hearer, that prepares him for the fight against the passions and against the activities of opposing powers, that prepares him for the heavenly festivals (for it is said with a view to both)—is taken as a trumpet.
comments.selected_reason: Says in one sentence what the trumpet stands for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The word does not want us to enter an unwalled city but the church of the living God, walled by the strength of the Word, and whoever stands outside will be caught by the enemies.
comments.comment: So the word says: 'Signal with a trumpet upon the earth, and cry aloud; say: Gather yourselves and let us enter the walled cities.' (Jeremiah 4:5) The word of God does not want us to enter an unwalled city, but into the church of the living God, walled by the strength of the Word—for he is the wall. … 'Taking it up, flee into Zion.' As many of you as are outside Zion, 'taking it up, flee into Zion; hurry, do not stand still.' (Psalm 9:11 (LXX)) You who are in progress, hurry to the Lookout, 'for I am bringing evils from the north and a great crushing' (Psalm 139:12 (LXX))—evils brought 'from the north'—from the opposing one, the north, as has often been said. Whoever is found not hurrying and not entering 'into the walled cities,' not becoming 'in the churches of God,' but standing outside, will himself be caught by the enemies and destroyed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the call to enter the walled cities and flee to Zion.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lion that has gone up from his den is the devil, the enemy we must flee, who as Peter teaches walks about like a roaring lion and lies in wait in secret, at night.
comments.comment: Who is the enemy? Let us see from what follows how it is said: 'A lion has gone up from his den; destroying nations he has carried them off.' This is the enemy we must flee. A lion pursues us. Who is this? Peter teaches, saying: 'Your adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion seeking whom he may swallow (1 Peter 5:8); resist him, firm in the faith.' And according to the ninth Psalm he 'lies in wait in secret; he lies in wait like a lion in his den.' And this lion does not lie in wait by day, but when night has come.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The lion has gone up from the place of his punishment to make your land a desolation, but you, being human, are higher than the devil, who is below because of wickedness.
comments.comment:
'A lion has gone up from his den.' … Where? When? He is down, having fallen; he has come down into the lowest parts of the earth. 'A lion has gone up from his den.' You are a human being; you are higher than the devil. For you are stronger than he, whatever you may be. He, because of wickedness, is below. So 'a lion has gone up from his den; destroying nations he has carried them off.' … Having gone up from his den—the place belonging to his own punishment—'destroying nations he has carried them off; he has gone out from his place to make your land a desolation.' … He wants your land, about which we spoke a little earlier. He wants each of us to be pastured on.

So he comes 'to make your land' desolate, so that the lion may trample the seeds, so that he may make your land empty. 'And your cities will be torn down because they are not inhabited.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains who the lion is and what he wants of the reader's land.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria
