comments.capsule: Since the lion threatens to wipe out your land, gird on sackcloth, weep and pray, so that God may destroy the lion and the wrath of his anger may turn away from you.
comments.comment: Since then a lion has gone up and a lion threatens you and wants to wipe out your land, gird sackcloth, weep and mourn, call on God through prayers, that he may destroy this lion from you and you may not fall into his mouth. For 'as when the shepherd snatches from a lion's mouth two legs or a lobe of an ear'—this lion seeks to take you by the ears, so that by your greediness, casting false words beside you, he may drive you from the truth; he wants to snatch your feet from the truth and devour them. But you gird sackcloth and beat your breast and weep and cry out, seeing the enemy who has come, so that 'the wrath of the Lord's anger' may turn away from you …
comments.selected_reason: Says what putting on sackcloth is for.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When God wished to exact justice from Israel, he told Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for a man doing judgment and seeking faith, and the brightness of the saints can procure that the very sinful are not punished at once.
comments.comment: And indeed those from Israel, having bent unrestrainedly unto disobedience, and leaving nothing of the base things unpracticed, necessarily provoked the lawgiver against themselves; and when he already wished to exact justice of the daring from those who had so fiercely grieved him, the prophet Jeremiah was bringing forward the petitions. And what does God say toward this? ‘Run round,’ he says, ‘in Jerusalem’s roads (Jeremiah 5:1), and see and know, and seek in her squares, if you find a man—if there is one doing judgment and seeking faith—and I will be gracious to them, says the Lord.’ And he said he would also remit for Sodom the justice through fire, if some five were in them holy and good. Therefore the saints’ brightness sometimes also procures for those very sinful the need not to be punished at once, as it were entreating the divine temper and checking the anger; …
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 4

comments.capsule: The eyes of the Lord are on faith as they are on the righteous, and so on hope, love, power, self-control, righteousness and every virtue, so whoever wants God's gaze must acquire the virtues.
comments.comment:
"Lord," he says, "your eyes are on faith" (Jeremiah 5:3). Just as "the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous" (Psalm 34:15), for he turns them away from the unrighteous, so the eyes of the Lord are on faith, for he turns them away from unbelief. So someone who understands what he is saying in prayer rightly says, "Lord, your eyes are on faith." That is what is written here: "Lord, your eyes are on faith." But since "if someone with understanding hears a wise saying, he will praise it and add to it" (Sirach 21:15), see how much can be drawn from "Lord, your eyes are on faith." Paul says, "These three now remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love" (1 Corinthians 13:13). As the eyes of the Lord are on faith, so the eyes of the Lord are on hope, and the eyes of the Lord are on love.

And since there is "a spirit of power and love and self-control" (2 Timothy 1:7), the eyes of the Lord are on love, and likewise the eyes of the Lord are on power and on self-control. … The eyes of the Lord are on righteousness. In this way, the eyes of the Lord are on every virtue. So if you too want the rays of God's spiritual eyes to reach you, take up the virtues. Then, just as we say, "Lord, your eyes are on faith," we can say, "Lord, your eyes are on" each good thing you acquire. And if you have grown so far that the Lord's eyes shine upon you, you will say, "The light of your face has been marked upon us, Lord" (Psalm 4:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the Lord's eyes are on faith and how a reader can come under his gaze.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's chastisements chastise the mind and bring a felt sense of what was sinned, and those who suffer from them are blessed while those who do not suffer are evil.
comments.comment:
Then regarding the sinners, let us consider what is said: 'You have chastised them and they did not suffer. These are the sensible chastisements offered to bodies, whether the afflicted will or not, causing them pain; but the chastisements of God are such that some of the afflicted suffer, and some of the afflicted do not.' (Jeremiah 5:3)

Let us see if we can explain what it means to suffer from God's chastisements and what it means not to suffer, and that those who do not suffer from God's chastisements are evil, but those who suffer are blessed. For Wisdom says: 'Who will give me a chastisement upon my mind and a seal upon my lips of deceitful ones, that I may not be ashamed of my ignorance, and my sins may not destroy me?' (Sirach 23:2) Pay attention to 'Who will give me a chastisement upon my mind?' Does not this mean that the mind is chastised? The chastisements of the Lord chastise the mind; for a word that lays hold of the soul and brings it to a felt sense of what has been sinned, and so scourges it. But the chastisements chastise the blessed one suffering upon the chastisements, for the things said are fulfilled in him, and he does not despise the one rebuking him from himself.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who hear reproof without blushing have hardened their faces, in the soul as in Pharaoh's heart, and the poor are those who do not wish to be taught the way of the Lord.
comments.comment:
They have hardened their faces above the rock; understand this from the more physical. Those who hear reproving words about sin blush and sink down and fall beneath the word of their reprover. But those are such that they are unblushing, not ashamed of what they are reproved for, what they have sinned. Therefore, if you were to speak about those who do not blush, 'They have hardened their faces above the rock,' (Jeremiah 5:3–5) if you have understood this upon the physical, turn with me in the word to the soul's face, about which it is said, 'Then face to face.' And see a firm soul, such as the heart of Pharaoh, hardened so that it stands as a counterpart to what is spoken and as if rejecting what is said, not shaped according to what is spoken.

For there you will find that 'They have hardened their faces above the rock and did not wish to turn back.' (Jeremiah 5:3) And I said, 'Perhaps they are poor, because they did not wish to know the way of the Lord and the judgment of God.' I will go to the stout and speak to them. Understanding this about those who do not wish to be taught, who do not understand the stripes of God, he says having understood their cause. Their soul is poor. 'And I said, 'Perhaps they are poor, because they could not, because they did not know the way of the Lord and the judgment of God.' 'I will go to the stout and speak to them.' The stout are called in praise of the soul. And among the Hellenes the term 'stout' is constantly used for the greatness of the rational soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God measures punishments with mercy, adding them in stages as Leviticus records, because he wants to lead the transgressor to repentance and not to destroy him.
comments.comment: The one judging the condemned grants place and does not immediately bear the end of punishment upon the transgressor. Therefore, 'judging briefly, he punishes.' This is exemplified in Leviticus, where prior punishments are recorded before subsequent penalties. The Lord says, 'If you do not turn back, I will add seven more plagues.' (Leviticus 26:18) Another punishment is again described: 'If you do not turn back, but go astray, I will go with you in a sideways manner.' (Leviticus 26:23-24) You will find God measuring punishments with mercy, as He desires to lead the transgressor to repentance, not wholly destroying them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the verse says God will not make an end in those days.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Although someone might say there was no end even with Nebuchadnezzar's captivity, the end of the people is in the presence of the Lord Jesus Christ, who wept over Jerusalem and left its house desolate.
comments.comment: The end upon Jerusalem was when the captivity of Nebuchadnezzar occurred. Although someone might say that even then there was no end, nor upon the Maccabees. But the end of the people is upon the presence of my Lord Jesus Christ. For the Savior did not say to them, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' as He did not forgive them. When He wept over Jerusalem, saying, 'Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often I desired to gather your children as a bird gathers its brood under its wings, and you would not!' 'Behold, your house is left to you desolate.' The house is left, surrounded by armies of Jerusalem, as the desolation of it has drawn near. Then after their transgression, salvation came to us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Punishments differ in number, for the seven plagues are inflicted one by one, and some are struck with seven and others with fewer, and God knows the plagues.
comments.comment: I consider that for us also such things may be, and some punishments may occur, so that these may not have a second punishment but be satisfied with the first, others may come even to the second, not indeed to the third, others may come even to the fourth. For the 'I will add seven plagues' (Leviticus 26:21) signifies a mystery of one by one being inflicted, and the second, and the third, up to the seven mentioned for some. Not all are struck with seven plagues; rather, some I suppose will be struck with seven, others with five, others with four, others with three or two, and the most helpless among all in punishments I consider to be struck with one. Therefore, God knows the things regarding the plagues. Hence it is written here at the beginning of the reading: 'And it will be in those days... I will not make an end for you. Not an end in those days; for there are some days when He will make those He wills for an end.' (Jeremiah 5:18)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sons of Israel, who had the land, the temple and the house of prayer, became idolaters, and anyone in the church who worships other gods will likewise be cast into a foreign land to worship the gods he once served.
comments.comment:
And it will be when you say, 'For what reason did the Lord God do all these evils to us?' (Jeremiah 5:19) And you will say to them, 'Because you abandoned me and served other gods in your land, so in a land not your own.' (Matthew 6:24)

The sons of Israel had the holy land, the temple, the house of prayer. They should have worshipped God. Transgressing the divine commands, they became idolaters and took in idols from Damascus, as written in the Books, and other idols from the land. … If anyone in the church of God, while present, worships other gods, making unworthy things divine, they will be cast into a foreign land to worship the gods they once served. Let the greedy be expelled from the church, and the glutton be outside the church.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Israel was sent into a foreign land and what it warns the reader.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A man can have eyes and yet not see soundly, either by seeing what is good and turning his will aside or by ruining his own mind in a hunt after notions about God, and seeing is of no use unless one sees soundly.
comments.comment: For some, he means, see what is good, yet turn the bent of their own wills aside toward what they ought not; others, though they could have a share in right doctrine, all but ruin their own minds themselves: they throw themselves into a most unlovely hunt after notions and accept nothing sound in their belief about God. Such above all are the children of the heretics, and the Jews besides, who believe that the Father is God, yet most foolishly thrust away the One who has come forth from him, the Son by nature. So the word proclaimed by the voice of the prophet is true of them: ‘They have eyes, and they do not see’ (Jeremiah 5:21). For seeing is of no use unless care is taken that one sees soundly, just as we rightly said that lameness and the crushed foot are placed on the same footing. For it will make no difference at all whether one cannot walk at all or perhaps does not walk soundly, meaning, of course, the path of conduct and the road of deeds.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: The sea, however it rages, dissolves its force into foam the moment it touches the shore, so that what cannot be withstood is bridled by the weakest thing, sand, and by the command of its Creator.
comments.comment: That is why the sea, even when it rages under the winds and its waves rear up to an enormous height, the moment it touches the shore, dissolves its force into foam and turns back. "Will you not fear me, says the Lord, who set the sand as a boundary for the sea?" (Jeremiah 5:22). The sea, whose violence cannot be withstood, is bridled by the weakest thing of all—sand. What else kept the Red Sea from sweeping over all Egypt, which lies lower than the sea itself, and joining the ocean that borders Egypt, if it was not bound by the command of its Creator?
comments.selected_reason: Shows concretely how sand can hold back the sea.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: We ourselves cause our suffering by whetting the Master to anger, so that he lets a man go toward a weak and cowardly mind, as in the weakness he gives this people.
comments.comment: But we ourselves are causes of the suffering to ourselves, whetting the Master of all into angers; for so he lets a man go toward a weak and cowardly mind. Or do you not hear him crying through one of the holy prophets: 'Behold, I give weakness upon this people, and they shall be weak in it, fathers and sons; neighbor and his neighbor shall perish' (Jeremiah 6:21)? And the most wise Paul also writes about some: 'And as they did not approve to have God in knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do the things that are not fitting.' (Romans 1:28)
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 1

comments.capsule: Jeremiah mourned that the Jews would not accept cleansing through Christ, and since silver cannot be cleansed without lead, Christ, who has cleansed us, is likened to lead.
comments.comment: … indeed the prophet Jeremiah was bewailing the peoples of the Jews not accepting the cleansing through Christ, saying: ‘The bellows has failed from fire, lead has failed; in vain a silversmith silversmiths; their evils have not been melted; call them rejected silver, because the Lord has rejected them.’ (Jeremiah 6:29–30) You understand therefore how divine Scripture has not been ignorant that the cleansing upon silver is not able to be practiced without lead. Therefore since Christ has thoroughly cleansed us being unapproved, he is likened to lead …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the refining image of lead and silver in the verse.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 3

comments.capsule: Gehenna, the place of punishment named in the Gospel, is found in the old writings as the Valley of the son of Ennom, which lies in the lot of the tribe of Benjamin, where Jerusalem also lay.
comments.comment: Now since we found Gehenna written in the Gospel as a place of punishment (Matthew 5:22; 10:28), we searched whether it was named anywhere in the old writings, especially since the Jews too use the name. We found that in some places Scripture calls it the “Valley of the son of Ennom” (Jeremiah 7:31–32); but in the Hebrew, as we have learned, where “Valley” stands, “the Valley of Ennom” and “Gehenna” were used of one and the same place. Keeping close watch on the readings, we find also that Gehenna, or the Valley of Ennom, is listed in the lot of the tribe of Benjamin, in which Jerusalem also lay (Joshua 18:16, 28).
comments.selected_reason: Shows where the name Gehenna comes from in this passage.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Resurrection happens to the soul and to the body: the sinner is dead and is awakened into the life that was before the fall, and the body, whose corruption came after its formation, rises too.
comments.comment: A resurrection occurs both according to the soul and according to the body; 'Awake, sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you' (Ephesians 5:14). Here, the one sinning is dead; for 'the soul, the one sinning, this one shall die' (Ezekiel 18:4); and: 'sin, having been completed, brings death' (James 1:15) to the one sinning. Therefore, awaken this one into the life that was before the fall; for this was the life with virtue. Thus also in Jeremiah it is said: 'Does not he who has fallen rise again?' (Jeremiah 8:4); and a resurrection also happens to the body; for its formation was not its fall, but the corruption after the formation. Therefore also it itself rises.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what rising again after a fall means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even a man whose soul is strengthened by human wisdom and reasoning is nothing if he rejects the word of God.
comments.comment: For even if someone has a soul strengthened by a morsel of human wisdom and by human reasonings, but rejects the word of God, it is nothing, and it will be accounted as nothing. Therefore the prophet says: 'They have done away with the word of the Lord' (Jeremiah 8:9). What wisdom is in them?
comments.author: Severianus of Gabala
comments.work: On the Blind Man and Zacchaeus

comments.capsule: Speaking peace while holding enmity is hypocrisy, which the Savior condemned and which makes an evil done to a brother a sin against God.
comments.comment:
"Each one speaks peace to his neighbor, but holds enmity within himself," and so on (Jeremiah 9:8). The scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people would not have inherited so great a "woe" from the Savior if it were not for hypocrisy. For in exposing their sins, the Lord never stopped warning them on every occasion: "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites," calling them whitewashed tombs, which appear beautiful to people on the outside but inside are full of dead bones and every kind of uncleanness (Matthew 23:27). If we do something good to a neighbor through unhypocritical love, we hear from the Savior: "Whatever you did for one of the least of these brothers of mine, you did for me" (Matthew 25:40). In the same way, if we do something evil to a brother through deceptive and defiled hypocrisy, or through any other sin whatever, we sin against God just as much. Hypocrisy, brothers, is therefore a terrible and hostile thing.

And deceit hidden in the heart, meant to entrap those who come forward in simplicity, speaks one thing with the mouth while carrying another in the breast, and so it deceives those who possess love.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse's hidden enmity amounts to and why the Savior condemned it.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: A truly peaceful man does not speak peaceably while holding another intention, and those who bring the divided into harmony are peacemakers, sons of God.
comments.comment: This indeed is also said in Jeremiah concerning someone: 'He speaks peaceably to his neighbor, but holds enmity within himself' (Jeremiah 9:8). 'To me,' he says, 'they spoke peaceably.' They did not simply speak 'peaceably,' but 'to me'; wanting to deceive me, they spoke peaceably; for the truly peaceful man does not speak peaceably to someone while holding another intention against him. Immediately also the Savior says to others that 'the peacemakers are blessed,' 'because they are sons of God' (Matthew 5:9). To be peaceful is to be sons of God. And he said 'peacemakers' to mean those making peace. When they lead those who have been divided by intention into harmony and friendship, they are peacemakers. And they are peacemakers toward themselves also.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Not even wisdom, strength or wealth is a ground for boasting, and one should boast as Paul did, in the cross and in his weaknesses.
comments.comment: Hear the word of the prophet Jeremiah commanding us not to boast even in wisdom: 'Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom,' (Jeremiah 9:23) he says, 'nor the strong in his strength, nor the rich in his wealth, but let the one who boasts boast in this: understanding and knowing that I am the Lord.' Do you want to boast and, boasting, not hear 'Be ashamed of your boasting'? Boast as the apostle and say: 'Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me and I to the world.' (Galatians 6:14) Do you want to boast so that it may not be said, 'Be ashamed of your boasting'? Hear Paul boasting and learn when he says: 'Most gladly then will I boast in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may tabernacle upon me.' Hear what kinds of boasts he boasts: 'In labors more abundantly'—which of us can say this?—'in prisons beyond measure, in deaths often.'
comments.selected_reason: Gives concrete examples of what to boast in and what not to.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Every good thing comes from God, so the one who boasts should boast only in knowing that the Lord shows mercy, judgment and righteousness.
comments.comment: Pride is not good, since it carries with it much empty glory. For it is clear—very clear—that every perfect good comes from God. It cannot be received by a human being in any other way, so that what has been said is truly the most certain of all: the one who boasts should glory only in this, in understanding and knowing that the Lord himself is the one who shows mercy and judgment and righteousness, and in this is the will of God (Jeremiah 9:24). For the divine takes pleasure in such a person and always produces good things that are lasting and secure, when that person attributes the cause of the good things he has to the one who is truly the ultimate cause—the one to whom he must also attribute the cause of the good things remaining.
comments.selected_reason: Says in plain terms why the verse allows boasting only in the Lord.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Peoples such as Edom, Ammon and Moab are called circumcised by the sacred word, yet they keep only an outward pretense of righteousness without cutting out evil.
comments.comment:
What was said a little earlier about Ishmael, that he received the law of circumcision from his father and handed it down to his own descendants, we may also say about Esau. He was the son of Isaac, the son of Abraham, and the law that came to him from his grandfather and his father he also handed down to his children. He himself circumcised Edom. Is this no longer unclear?

And how are the sons of Ammon and the sons of Moab circumcised? Those who have studied more carefully know that these are the sons of Lot, Abraham's nephew. … All these things, once said, persuade us without difficulty to agree that all these peoples are called circumcised by the sacred word. The sacred word itself testifies through Jeremiah about the sons of Moab and the sons of Ammon, that he counted them among the circumcised. … If we should gain some benefit from these words, we may rightly say that many peoples of the human race have a pretense of righteousness and bear certain traces of the law of God. They are shaped in some way and superficially cultivate virtue. Yet their resolve stops at outward form, at pretense and hypocrisy. They did not even strive to cut out evil from themselves, as the reproaches against Egypt and Idumea, that is Edom, show.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Jeremiah counts these nations among the circumcised.
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: Spiritual circumcision belongs to the one who has God, for Jeremiah says that all the Gentiles are uncircumcised in the flesh but the house of Israel in their hearts.
comments.comment: It must be considered what the spiritual circumcision is, which one having God is circumcised, not necessarily one being circumcised according to the flesh. For the prophet says to those striving only according to the flesh: 'Be circumcised to your God, and do not circumcise the flesh of your uncircumcision' (Jeremiah 4:4); and the same prophet says: 'All Gentiles are uncircumcised in the flesh, but the house of Israel are uncircumcised in their hearts' (Jeremiah 9:26). Therefore, he who is sensibly circumcised removes something of that which serves the generation of the member, just as he who casting out every thought friendly to the generation of the intellect circumcises the heart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Rather than learn the ways of the nations, one learns God's law, which forbids other gods.
comments.comment: "Do not learn according to the ways of the nations." And what do you learn? You learn the law of God, which says: "You shall have no other gods besides me." "Let the gods who did not make heaven and earth perish from the face of the earth and from under heaven" (Jeremiah 10:11).
comments.author: Gregory Thaumaturgus

comments.capsule: A man's way is not his own in two senses: God can block even a great man's course against us, and though we can will to run the saving way, the directing and guiding come from God.
comments.comment:
Again, if it is said in Jeremiah (Jeremiah 10:23), do not think it as an opposition: 'I know that the way of man is not his own, nor does a man direct his steps.' The prophet's meaning is twofold. Nebuchadnezzar threatens the destruction of Jerusalem and the deportation of the whole Hebrew race. The prophet said that, even if the threat existed and we ourselves provided the causes for this to be suffered, 'I know that the way of man is not his own' (Jeremiah 10:23). You are able to prevent his way against us; for even if a man is thought to be great, his course is not made straight if you prevent it.

It is also possible to take it according to the meaning already assigned to: 'not by the willer or the runner, but by the God who shows mercy' (Romans 9:16). Set your intention to run the saving way. It is not within our power to run the way, but to will to arrive at the end of the way, so as to say: 'I have finished the race' (2 Timothy 4:7). From Him is the directing, from Him is the guiding. 'Lead me in your truth' (Psalm 25:5). The one being led by God does not make himself straight. But he intends to be made straight and has given himself to the One who is able to lead him into perfection.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to understand the verse so that it does not seem to contradict other sayings.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's wrath is no passion but a stern discipline for those who have sinned much, as the Psalm and Jeremiah's prayer for discipline in judgment, not anger, show.
comments.comment: We do, then, speak of the wrath of God; but we say that it is not a passion of his. It is something employed to discipline, by sterner methods, those who have committed sins so many and of such a kind. That what is called the wrath of God, and what is named his anger, disciplines, and that this is the teaching of the Word, is clear from what is said in the sixth Psalm: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath” (Psalm 6:1); and in Jeremiah: “Discipline us, Lord, but with judgment and not in anger, lest you make us few” (Jeremiah 10:24).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Having played the harlot and disregarded the spiritual Bridegroom, the Synagogue became fuel for the fire, and Jeremiah weeps over her as the olive tree set alight.
comments.comment: [Of the Synagogue of the Jews:] Having played the harlot, then, and utterly disregarded the spiritual Bridegroom from above, she has become fuel for the fire. So the prophet Jeremiah too sheds bitter tears over her and says: ‘A beautiful olive tree, well shaded in appearance: so the Lord called your name. At the sound of its circumcision a fire was kindled against it; great is the affliction upon you. Its branches have become useless, and the Lord of hosts, who planted you, has pronounced evil against you.’ (Jeremiah 11:16–17) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains whom the burned olive tree stands for and why.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria
comments.work: On Adoration and Worship in Spirit and Truth, Book 12

comments.capsule: Kidneys, like the heart, name where the mind brings forth, and God is far from these, not from the bodily parts.
comments.comment: Therefore there are also wombs, according to that which the soul or the mind brings forth; those he calls kidneys along with the named heart. 'You are near,' he says, 'to their mouth, but far from their kidneys' (Jeremiah 12:2). From these kidneys you are far, O God, not from the physical parts.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord's inheritance, the people once placed in Paradise, turned wild and now nests among fruitless trees, like a lion in a forest.
comments.comment: And 'from the horns of the unicorns my humiliation' he can say here, referring to the multitude of the Jews, the people of Israel; for he said in Jeremiah: 'I have forsaken my house, I have left my inheritance. My inheritance became to me like a lion in a forest' (Jeremiah 12:7). Having been a people whom I placed in Paradise, where there was much fruit, when they had turned into wildness, then consequently they nest in fruitless trees—for the forest is nothing other than a place of fruitless trees. Therefore, they encamp there. And my inheritance, which I had so that it might be a people and a portion of the Lord, was so provoked against me as to be thrown upon a lion, not a lion being tamed—for often lions come into human places being tamed—but as in a forest, as a wild beast.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the lion in the forest as the people turned wild.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Christ is the speaker, and the land was desolated after the people killed the Christ of God.
comments.comment: Who is the one saying, 'Through me the whole land was made desolate with desolation' (Jeremiah 12:11)? Christ says these things. Before his sojourn many sins had indeed come to the people, but not of such a kind that they should be abandoned altogether and handed over to a long captivity. But when they filled up 'the measure of their fathers' (Matthew 23:32 … ) and added to killing the prophets and pursuing the righteous the killing of 'the Christ of God,' then what was spoken came to be: 'Your house is left to you.' And because of him they have suffered these things, and 'with desolation the whole land was made desolate.' (Matthew 23:38)
comments.selected_reason: Says who speaks the verse and why the land was made desolate.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: On a higher reading, the earth in the believer is made desolate when Jesus comes, because the members upon the earth are put to death and the flesh no longer works its own works.
comments.comment: But if you also want to hear something higher than 'Through me the whole land was made desolate with desolation,' (Jeremiah 12:11) look at the earth in you—how it was made desolate when Jesus came. For it was made desolate when 'the members that are upon the earth' (Colossians 3:5) were put to death, and the earth no longer works its own works. No longer do the works of the flesh spring up in the righteous, with which the flesh used to flourish—no longer fornication, no longer uncleanness, no longer sensuality, no idolatry, no sorcery, and the rest. And the Savior also says: 'Do you think that I came to cast peace upon the earth? I did not come to cast peace but a sword.' (Matthew 10:34) Truly, before he came there was no sword upon the earth, nor did 'the flesh desire against the Spirit, nor the Spirit against the flesh.' But when he came and we were taught what belongs to the flesh and what to the Spirit, the teaching, become like a sword on earth, divided the flesh and the earth from the Spirit. And 'the earth was made desolate' when we carry about the putting-to-death of Jesus in the body, and we no longer live according to flesh, but the Spirit lives, and we sow nothing into the flesh but everything into the Spirit, so that we may not reap corruption from the flesh but from the Spirit eternal life.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a reading of the desolated land that a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who handle God's oracles without living or believing as they ought sow wheat and reap thorns, and their lots do not benefit them.
comments.comment: It is said to those who have sinned: 'Sow wheat and reap thorns.' (Jeremiah 12:13 … ) For even if they deal with the oracles of God, those who do not deal with them well, nor live as they ought, nor believe, sow wheat and reap thorns. Especially this can be understood of the heterodox who meet the Scriptures and reap thorns not from the Scriptures but from their own inventions. 'Their lots will not benefit them.' (Jeremiah 12:13 … ) Others have also explained these things. And since we do not reject their explanation, we fairly bring it into the open—not as ourselves discovering it but as having learned a good lesson. This word will benefit both you and us if we pay attention to what is written—we who seem to be of a certain lot, seated in front of you, so that some want to come into this lot.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what sowing wheat and reaping thorns means here.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Being in a lot does not save, for elders may perish and lay people be blessed, and more is required of those given the greater trust.
comments.comment:
But know that the lot does not save in every case. For many elders too will perish, and many of the laity will be shown blessed.

Since then there are some in the lot who do not live so as to be benefited and to adorn the lot, therefore, say those who explained it, it is written: 'Their lots will not benefit them.' For what benefits is not the mere sitting in the eldership, but living worthily of the place, as the word requires. The word requires you also to live well, and us. But if one may put it so—'the mighty will be examined mightily' … more is required of me than of the deacon, more of the deacon than of the layperson, and the one entrusted with the rule of us all, the church's rule itself, is required still more. Therefore the apostle who was entrusted with great things says—listen—'Let a person regard us as servants of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God.' … Here then seek among the stewards that someone faithful be found. And so rare it is to find a steward faithful and good.

Jesus, 'who knows all things before their coming to be,' says: 'Who then is the faithful and prudent steward, whom his lord will set over his household to give the measure of grain to his servants in season?' Then he blames certain stewards and says: 'But if that wicked servant begins to say, “My lord delays to come,” and begins to beat his fellow servants and the maidservants, and to eat and drink and get drunk, the lord of that servant will come on a day he does not expect and at an hour he does not know, and will cut him in two, and assign his portion with the unfaithful.' So much for 'Their lots will not benefit them.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Boasting in riches and in things that are not worth boasting about calls for the rebuke to be ashamed of one's boasting.
comments.comment: Let us also look at the necessary rebuke next, which it is good to take up in the ethical place, saying: 'Be ashamed of your boasting, of reproach before the Lord.' (Jeremiah 12:13) There are things in which we boast through folly, though they are not worthy of boasting. For example, if someone boasts that he is rich and possesses much, one might say to him: 'Be ashamed of your boasting.' …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Linen rises from the earth and must be carded, washed and scrubbed to turn from dark to bright, as we must be before we are woven onto God's belt.
comments.comment: And why also 'linen'? Because it has its origin from earth; for it is a plant rising from earth, then after being cultivated it is carded and washed and scrubbed and made with much working, so that it may become such as to be a belt or whatever else. We too then all have our origin as God's belt, and having our origin from earth we need much preparation, that we may be carded, that we may be washed, that we may put away the color of the earth. For the color of linen's origin is one thing, and that from the working another. The color of linen's origin is rather black, but from the working it becomes most bright. Something of this kind also reaches us who are in generation. We are black according to the beginning in believing; therefore at the beginning of the Song of Songs it is said: 'I am black and beautiful.' And we at the start resemble Ethiopians in the soul. Then we are scrubbed clean, that we may become brighter according to 'Who is this who comes up whitened?' And we become 'bright and clean linen,' then also we are woven onto God's belt when we are worthy to be glued to God. God does not put us away. He put away the first people—'the whole house of Judah' and 'the house of Israel.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet's belt was linen.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The people is God's covering and shield against accusers, and the one who sins is cast from God's waist and destroyed at the Euphrates.
comments.comment: [God glues the belt around his waist.] To what end? That it may be shown that the people is as it were a covering of God. For against those who want to accuse God the people stands and as it were shields him and does not allow anything out of place to be said about God. But when we sin, just as the prophet puts this belt away and condemns it to the Euphrates river so that it may be destroyed there, so the one who sins is cast away from God's waist, and having been cast out is thrown into the Euphrates river—the river of Mesopotamia, where the Assyrians are enemies to Israel, where the Babylonians are—and there he is destroyed. For though there are so many rivers, the prophet is sent from Judea to the Euphrates river to deal with and lead away a linen belt.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the belt is hidden at the Euphrates and what it means for those who sin.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The rotten belt is Israel, which God glued to himself to be a people, a boast and a glory, with the prophet standing in God's place.
comments.comment: After days he [the prophet] goes there and finds this belt rotten. And the Lord adds, giving the occasion for interpreting the belt, saying: 'As the belt is glued to a man's waist, so I glued to myself the house of Israel and the whole house of Judah, says the Lord, to become for me a people named and a boast and a glory—and they did not listen to me.' So the prophet is taken in God's place, girding the linen belt around his waist, as God girded the people: 'For I glued this people to myself,' he says—as if the people becomes God's belt.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God no longer girds the first people but has woven another belt, the church from the nations, which must fear being cast off if she sins.
comments.comment: It [the first belt, the former people] came to be so as not to be used any longer; for he no longer girds them around himself. In their place God has girded us; for having cast off the belt he did not remain naked, but wove another belt for himself. This belt is the church from the nations—which should know that 'if God did not spare the former, how much more will he not spare her either if she sins,' (Romans 11:21) unless she is worthy of God's waist. 'But the one glued to the Lord is one spirit' in Christ Jesus …
comments.selected_reason: Says whom the belt now stands for after Israel is put away.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: From the waist down God is fire and above it electrum, so those in generation need fire's cleansing and those who progress become the electrum around his higher body.
comments.comment:
But why does it become God's belt around his waist? Let the one able, reading Ezekiel and seeing God as it were embodied by the word—and how what is from the waist downward is fire, and what is from the waist is electrum—search out the word, why what is below God is fire. The matters from the waist and from generation—these are fire. For everything in generation needs the cleansing that comes from fire; everything in generation needs chastisement. But what is above the waist and has gone beyond generation—these are matter as in what is purest and most precious; for electrum is said to be more valuable than gold.

Since then Scripture uses examples in order to teach that God's body above is more honorable and the body below is lesser, for this reason it introduced God composed of fire and electrum. And each of us in generation is fire; we are not the electrum. But if we ascend and make progress—for it is possible to move from being today among the things below, so as to become God's body above—we will be, having crossed the fire, the electrum around God's higher body. So he glues around his waist the linen belt.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Read as a bare letter the saying seems foolish, but each wineskin, good or wicked, is filled with its own kind of wine according to its goodness or wickedness.
comments.comment:
What the prophet is commanded by God to say ought to be worthy of God. Yet if we remain on the letter it does not appear worthy of God, so that someone hearing the letter might say: these letters are folly. But a psychic person will say this; for 'the psychic person does not receive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are folly to him.' (1 Corinthians 2:14)

Look then at what the wording says. 'And you shall say to this people: Thus says the Lord the God of Israel'—what 'the Lord the God of Israel' says, let it be worthy of the Lord of Israel—'Every wineskin will be filled with wine. And if they say to you, “Shall we not know, knowing, that every wineskin will be filled with wine?” (Jeremiah 13:12)' And those who answer, if they say these things standing on the bare wording, claim to know that 'every wineskin will be filled with wine,' and they lie. For not every wineskin will be filled with wine. There are wineskins filled with oil or with some other liquid substance. So some lie; for not every wineskin will be filled with wine. And the people answers saying: 'Shall we not know, knowing, that every wineskin will be filled with wine?'—words that will receive an interpretation of this kind, as far as we can.

If we know the differences among wines and what is said about them, and accordingly look at the wineskins, we will see that it is true that every wineskin will be filled with wine. For whether someone is good—let us name him so among wineskins, a wineskin—he will be filled with wine according to his own goodness. Or whether he is, by comparison of wineskins and the judgment about them, wicked, he too according to his wickedness will be filled with wicked wine. How then can we take from Scripture the different wines? About the worse ones it is written like this: 'For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and their shoot from Gomorrah.

Their grape is a grape of gall; a cluster of bitterness to them; their wine is the rage of dragons, and the incurable rage of asps.' And about the better ones: 'Your cup that makes drunk is as the strongest,' … and Wisdom calls to her own mixing-bowl saying: 'Come, eat my bread, and drink the wine I have mixed for you.' (Psalm 23:5 (LXX)) So there is wine from Sodom, and there is wine that Wisdom mixes. And again: 'A vineyard came to be for the beloved on a horn in a rich place,' planted by God, the vine called Sorek—choice and marvelous. And there is also a vine of the Egyptians, which God strikes according to what is written: that 'God struck their vine with hail, and their mulberry trees with frost.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the puzzling saying that every wineskin will be filled with wine.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God spares no one, priest or prophet, and as he scattered at Babel and scattered Israel after its sin, so he gathers the righteous and scatters sinners.
comments.comment: Then he teaches, for those who sinned—as far as the wording goes—then in Jerusalem and in Judea, with what sort of wine God fills these wineskins, the sinners. For it is written: 'If they say to you, “Not knowing, we will not know that every wineskin will be filled with wine,” (Jeremiah 13:12) you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Look, I fill all who inhabit this land and the kings sitting as sons of David on his throne and the priests.' The one about to punish spares no one. Not because someone was named a prophet, yet has sins, will he not be filled with the threats spoken. Not because someone was named a priest and seemed to have the superiority of a more honored name than the people does God spare him so that he is not punished when he has sinned. And the things written about those people, the apostle says, were written for us, 'upon whom the ends of the ages have come.' If then anyone among these priests also (I mean us elders) or among these Levites standing around the people (I mean the deacons) sins, he will have this punishment—as again there are certain priestly blessings, about which, God granting, not far off but after the examination of the prophetic word we will know when Numbers is read; for something about priests is about to be said there. So 'the priests' and 'the prophets and Judah and all who inhabit Jerusalem,' God says he will fill 'with drunkenness' and scatter 'them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons.' And let us understand these things thus: God gathers the righteous, but scatters the sinners. Therefore also when human beings had not moved from the east, God did not scatter them; but when they moved 'from the east' and 'a man said to his neighbor: Come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower whose head will be to heaven,' God says about them: 'Come, let us go down and confuse their tongue there,' and each is confused and scattered to some place of the earth. And the people of Israel, when not sinning, was in Judea; but having sinned is scattered afterward throughout the inhabited world and sown everywhere.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Sinners are punished by being kept from one another, and God disciplines those the word has not turned, as a master does, so that the pains may turn them.
comments.comment:
Think something of this kind with me also about all of us.

There is a 'church of firstborn enrolled in heaven,' (Hebrews 12:23) where is Mount Zion and city of the living God, heavenly Jerusalem. The blessed will be gathered there, that they may be together. But sinners are also punished in this: in not being with one another. I know some in this life who, for punishment, want to hand over to some island and, for torment, the household of someone who grieved the kingdom, scattering—here the wife, here the one son, then elsewhere the other—so that not even in the disaster the mother may enjoy the son, or the brother the brother. Think something of this kind also upon the unjust. You who are a sinner managed by God must taste something more bitter, that being disciplined you may be saved.

And just as you do not punish a household slave or son under your punishment simply wanting to torment him, but that by the pains you may turn him, so also God will discipline those not turned by the word, those not healed, with the pains from sufferings. For discipline he puts around what he puts around according to what is said: 'With toil and scourge you will always be disciplined, Jerusalem.' (Jeremiah 6:8) So that the disciplining pain may grow, those in pain are scattered from one another so that this one and that one may not be together. For the intensity of the pain would be loosened through the comfort of each toward what comes from the other (Ezekiel 20:23).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bad people together increase their evil, so God scatters them from one another that their wickedness may shrink.
comments.comment: But if another cause of being scattered must also be added to the account, I will set this beside it. Bad people being with one another look to the bad things and increase them, just as good people being with good ones consider good things. So the evil counsel is dissolved and divided—having been able to hold with the like—when the wicked are scattered from one another. For this reason God arranges that the worthless not be with one another, perhaps also providing for them, that their wickedness may not grow together but may shrink as it is dissolved. These things because of 'I will scatter them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons together. Says the Lord. I will not long for them and I will not spare and I will not pity from their destruction.' (Jeremiah 13:14)
comments.selected_reason: Gives a second reason why God scatters the wicked.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A judge or physician who spares one out of pity harms the many, so God, who manages the whole world, does not spare one for the sake of the common good.
comments.comment:
Those from the heresies mount upon such sayings and say: Do you see what the craftsman is like? The God of the prophets who says, 'I will not spare and I will not pity from their destruction' (Jeremiah 13:14)—how can this one be good? But if I take as an example a judge who for the common good does not pity and who rightly is not merciful, I will be able from the example to persuade that God, sparing many, does not spare one. And I will also take a physician as example, showing that sparing the whole body he does not spare one member. Let this be set before a judge: to craft peace and arrange what is beneficial for the nation under him. And let someone be brought forward, a murderer fair in appearance and beautiful to see. Let a mother come forward bringing pitiful words to the judge, that her old age may be pitied; let the wife of this one unworthy of pity beg; let children standing around plead about him.

Upon these things what benefits the common? That this one be pitied or not pitied? But if pitied he will return to the same things; if not pitied he himself will die, but the common will be improved. So if God spares the sinner and pities him and has compassion so as not to punish, who will not be worn down? Who of the worthless—those who through fear of punishments stop their sins—will not be worn down and become worse? Such things can also be seen happening in the churches: someone sinned; after the sin he begged about communion. If he is pitied too quickly, the common is worn down. The sin of others grows.

But if by reasoning—not as unmerciful nor as harsh the judge, but as providing also for the one, yet providing more for the many than for the one—he considers the coming damage to the common from the communion of the one and from the forgiveness of his sin, clearly he will cast out the one in order to save the many. Look with me also at a physician, how if he is sparing of cutting what must be cut, if sparing of cauterizing what must be cauterized because of the pains that follow such helps, how the disease grows and becomes worse.

But if he comes more boldly to the cutting and the burning, he will heal through not pitying, through seeming not to have compassion on that one being cauterized and cut. So also God does not manage one human being, but manages the whole world; he administers the things in heaven, the things on earth everywhere. He considers then what benefits the whole world and all that are; as far as possible he also considers what benefits the one—yet not so that the benefit of the one comes at the damage of the world. For this reason eternal fire was also prepared; for this reason Gehenna was also made ready; for this reason there is also an outer darkness—needed not only because of the one punished, but most of all because of the common (Matthew 25:41) (Matthew 5:22).
comments.selected_reason: Answers the objection of how a good God can say he will not spare.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The scourging of the pestilent one makes the foolish shrewd, so the punishment of some benefits the salvation of others.
comments.comment: But if you want to take Scripture as witness that sinners are punished also for the training of others, even if these at some time are given up as beyond healing, hear Solomon in the Proverbs saying: 'When a pestilent one is scourged, the foolish becomes more shrewd.' (Proverbs 19:25) He did not say that the one scourged himself will be more shrewd and more prudent through the scourgings, but that the foolish changes from folly to prudence through the scourgings applied to the pestilent one; for this is what the name of shrewdness signifies here. And the foolish changes by seeing others scourged. So it benefits us—if at least we become worthy of salvation through others being punished—the punishment of others. And as Israel's trespass benefited the salvation of the nations, so the punishment of some will benefit the salvation of others. For this reason God, being good, says: 'I will not spare and I will not pity from their destruction.' (Jeremiah 13:14)
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one has reasonable ground to exalt himself, whether over rank, wealth or even virtue and suffering for Christ, since Paul was given an angel of Satan to buffet him lest he be exalted.
comments.comment:
What I mean will be clear like this: there are some who exalt themselves because they are sons of governors and because they are of a family from great worldly ranks. Such people, exalting themselves over an involuntary and indifferent matter, do not even have a plausible likelihood that what is set beside them for exaltation is reasonable. There are those who exalt themselves because they have authority to kill human beings, and who exalt themselves because they have received what among them is called such a promotion that they cut off human heads. 'The glory' of such people 'is in their shame.' Others exalt themselves over wealth—not the true wealth but the one below; and others exalt themselves, say, over having a fine house or many fields. None of these is worthy of account; one must not exalt oneself over any of these.

But the plausible case about exaltation is when someone exalts himself because he is wise, and exalts himself knowing in himself that already for ten years he has not touched sexual things, or even from childhood has not touched them; and again another exalts himself because he wore bonds concerning Christ. There is a semblance here that suggests that someone reasonably exalts himself—yet even over these, as toward the true account, no one reasonably exalts himself. So there is no reasonable exaltation even over these.

Paul had the material for exaltation through visions, through sights, through wonders and signs, through the toils he toiled for Christ, through the churches he planted, ambitious where Christ was not named to found a church. All these were material for him, if one must speak with the semblance about exaltation, that to some it would have seemed fine for him to exalt himself. But still, since even exaltation over such things is not without danger, the kind Father, as he granted him visions and sights, so also gave him in the portion of a gift 'an angel of Satan to buffet him, that he may not be exalted beyond measure.' (2 Corinthians 12:7) And about this he begged the Lord three times that the angel of Satan depart from him—the one given him that he may not exalt himself. And the Lord answered him (for Paul was worthy of the Lord's answer) and said to him: 'My grace is enough for you; for my power is perfected in weakness.' (2 Corinthians 12:9 …)

So one must exalt oneself over nothing; for falling follows exaltation according to 'Before crushing a man's heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.' So much for 'Hear and give ear, and do not exalt yourselves, for the Lord has spoken.' (Jeremiah 13:15)
comments.selected_reason: Shows through examples why there is no ground for pride.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet asks both to hear and to give ear, the one received into the mind and the other into the ears, and then forbids exalting oneself.
comments.comment:
One chapter having been marked off, let us also see what the other teaches us: 'Hear and give ear, and do not exalt yourselves, for the Lord has spoken. Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble on dark mountains; and you will wait for light, and there is a shadow of death, and they will be placed into darkness.' (Jeremiah 13:16)

'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult, and your eyes will bring down tears, because the Lord's flock was crushed.' He wants the same people both to hear and to give ear, not content either with their hearing alone or with their giving ear. Therefore he says: 'Hear and give ear.' Then after this he commands them not to exalt themselves, and teaches what must be done. What then is hearing and what is giving ear? Let us understand from the wording itself. 'Give ear'—receive into the ears; and 'hear'—if it is said in distinction from 'give ear'—perhaps is: receive into the mind. And among the things said in the Scriptures some are more ineffable and more mystical, and some are useful at once to those who understand. About the more ineffable I think 'hear' is said; about those useful at once and able without interpretation to benefit the hearer, 'give ear.' So if we examine the whole Scripture we will say, becoming 'approved bankers': hear this, but give ear to that.

Then when we have heard and given ear, he commands us: 'And do not exalt yourselves.' (Jeremiah 13:15) For 'everyone who exalts himself will be humbled.' (Luke 14:11) And the Savior too, in saying, 'Learn from me that I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls,' (Matthew 11:29) teaches us not to exalt ourselves. For among the other human evils this sin also is much in us—sometimes exalting ourselves quite irrationally and over what one ought not exalt oneself even in the least, and sometimes with a semblance of reason, that what we exalt ourselves over is reasonable, yet even over that exaltation is not sound.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Give glory to God while the light is in you, since some darkening can come and one must not wait in it.
comments.comment: Let us also see what he commands us to do after these things: 'Give,' he says, 'glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains; and you will wait for light.' (Jeremiah 13:16) He wants the one giving 'glory to God' to give 'glory to God' while there is light, as if God's glory cannot be announced when it has grown dark and darkness has come. When then does it grow dark, and when does the darkening not come? 'Work while the light is in you.' (John 12:35) 'The light is in' you if you have in you the one who said: 'I am the light of the world.' As long as this rises for you, glorify God; but know that some darkening can come, and one must not remain in this darkening, but before the darkening give glory to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what giving glory before it grows dark means.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Bright mountains are the holy angels, prophets and apostles, and dark mountains are the devil and those who lift heights against the knowledge of God, on which the feet stumble.
comments.comment:
'Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains.' (Jeremiah 13:16) There are dark mountains; there are bright mountains. Bright mountains are the holy angels of God, the prophets, Moses the servant, the apostles of Jesus Christ. All these are bright mountains, and about these I think it has been said in the Psalms: 'His foundations are in the holy mountains.' (Psalm 87:1) And what are dark mountains? Those who lift up heights against the knowledge of God.

The devil is a dark mountain; the rulers of this age who are being abolished are dark mountains; and the demon of epilepsy was a mountain, and it was a dark mountain, about which the Savior said: 'You will say to this mountain.' For when the account of epilepsy was being sought and the disciples said, 'Why could we not cast it out?' the Savior answers that 'If you have faith as a mustard seed, you will say to this mountain' (Matthew 17:20)—about which you put forward the question, about which you sought—'You will say to this: Move from here to there, and it will move.' (Matthew 17:20) 'From here' from the human being, 'there' to its own place. So those who stumble do not stumble on bright mountains but on dark mountains, when they come to be with the devil and his angels, the dark mountains. 'And you will wait for light.' Yet it can also be joined to 'Give glory to the Lord our God'—the 'and you will wait for light.'

If you give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble on dark mountains, clearly even if it grows dark you will wait for the light and the light will succeed you. But another might say (I do not know whether understanding soundly or not) that even those who stumble 'on dark mountains' will wait among the dark mountains waiting for the light of mercy; for this will seem to be the 'and you will wait for light.' And when someone comes upon the dark mountains, let us see what is there: 'shadow of death.'

Where the dark mountains are, there is a shadow of death generated from the dark mountains themselves. 'And they will be placed into darkness.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the dark mountains on which feet stumble.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To hear in a hidden way is to grasp the spiritual meaning of the law and the parables, which one who keeps circumcision, Passover, unleavened bread, Sabbath or fast only openly has not done.
comments.comment:
'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' Of those who hear, some hear in a hidden way, and some, even if they hear, do not hear in a hidden way. What then is hearing in a hidden way but 'But we speak God's wisdom in a mystery, the hidden wisdom which God predetermined before the ages for our glory' (1 Corinthians 2:7)? And again elsewhere it is said that 'most of God's works are in hidden things.' If I hear the law, I either hear in a hidden way or I do not hear in a hidden way.

The Jew does not hear the law in a hidden way; therefore he is circumcised openly, not knowing that it is not 'the one who is a Jew openly, nor the circumcision openly in flesh.' But the one who hears circumcision in a hidden way will be circumcised in secret; the one who hears the things legislated about the Passover in a hidden way eats from the sheep of Christ—for 'our Passover was sacrificed, Christ'—and knowing what the flesh of the Word is like, and knowing that 'it is true food,' he partakes of it; for he heard the Passover in a hidden way. But this common Jew for this reason killed the Lord Jesus and is still today liable for Jesus' murder, since he heard neither the law nor the prophets in a hidden way.

If you read about the unleavened breads, one can hear the command in a hidden way, and one can hear it openly. As many of you as (for the Passover is near) keep unleavened breads, the bodily unleavened breads, you do not hear the command that says: 'If you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep.' And about the Sabbath women who have not heard the prophet do not hear in a hidden way but hear openly. They do not bathe on the Sabbath day; they return 'to the poor and weak elements,' as if Christ had not sojourned—the one who perfects us and carries us across from the legal elements to the Gospel perfection.

For this reason let us attend, reading the law and the prophets, lest we fall under the prophecy that says: 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' As many as keep the Jewish fast as not understanding the day of atonement after Jesus Christ's sojourn—you did not hear the atonement in a hidden way, but only openly; for to hear the atonement in a hidden way is to hear how God set Jesus as atonement for our sins, and that 'he is atonement for our sins, not for ours only but also for the whole world.' And even if Gospel parables are read and the hearer is one of those outside, he will not hear them in a hidden way.

But if the hearer is an apostle or one of those entering 'into Jesus' house,' he comes to Jesus, inquires also about the unclearness of the parable, and Jesus interprets it, and that hearer of the Gospel becomes one hearing it in a hidden way, so that his soul may not weep; for the soul of those not hearing in a hidden way weeps.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul weeps for not hearing in a hidden way, and since the Lord's flock was once crushed, those grafted in must fear lest it be crushed again and must seek its healing.
comments.comment:
How marvelously he did not say: you will weep, if you do not hear in a hidden way, but: 'your soul will weep.' There is a weeping of the soul alone weeping, and perhaps the Savior teaches us that weeping when he says: 'There will be the weeping.' And even if he says: 'Woe to those who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep,' he speaks about that weeping which the prophet also threatens here saying: 'But if you do not hear in a hidden way, your soul will weep from before insult.' For when you are insulted, then you will weep and your eyes will bring down tears, because the Lord's flock was crushed. If someone now sees the Jewish things and compares them with the ancient, he will see in what way the Lord's flock was crushed.

For this was once the Lord's flock, and since they judged themselves unworthy, the word turned to the nations. If then that flock of the Lord was crushed, we the wild olive, grafted contrary to its nature into the cultivated olive of the fathers—ought we not fear more, lest this 'flock of the Lord' also be crushed? For it is going to be crushed sometime according to what was said by the Savior, when 'because lawlessness is multiplied the love of many will grow cold.' About whom is the word? Is 'the love of many will grow cold' not said about those called Christians? About whom is the word, that 'When the Son of Man comes, will he find the faith on the earth?' (Luke 18:8) Is it not about us? For this reason let us attend to ourselves, doing everything, that day by day this flock of God may be improved, healed, cured, and every crushing depart from our souls, that we may be perfected in Christ Jesus …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The soul that has changed from Jebus [Trodden] into Jerusalem [Vision of peace] and then sins against Jesus will hear the same words: who will spare you?
comments.comment:
I move from the letter—though I have already taken the road the word gave—onto each soul already counted worthy to see peace. For after the divine lessons you have become Jerusalem, having formerly been Jebus. History says that one's name was Jebus; then second it changed the name and it became Jerusalem. Children of the Hebrews say Jebus is interpreted 'Trodden.'

So Jebus—the soul trodden by opposing powers—has been changed and has become Jerusalem, Vision of peace.

If then, when you changed from Jebus so as to become Jerusalem, you sinned and trampled the Son of God and counted the blood of the new covenant common (as that Jerusalem did, and you too) and are in hard sins, it will be said also about you: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?' (Jeremiah 15:5)—if you become such as to betray Jesus. Each of us, when we sin—and especially if the sins are greater—sins against Jesus. … let us do everything so that it may not also be said about us: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you? Or who will turn back to ask after your peace?'
comments.selected_reason: Gives a reader a clear picture of the verse applied to the Christian's own soul.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: No one, not even the angels, can plead for Jerusalem once her sin against Jesus is so great that God himself has passed judgment on it.
comments.comment:
We want to understand the words spoken to Jerusalem with much threat, which run like this: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? Or who will look gloomy over you? Or who will turn back to ask after your peace? You have turned away from me, says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 15:5) … I take as an example a certain enemy proved against the one who reigns on earth: that it is not permitted even to give him a share of mercy, lest someone seem to strike against the king who condemned him. And it is not permitted even to pity such a one. Some go further and do not even look gloomy over him, lest by looking gloomy they seem displeased at what the king judged. If you have understood this, look with me at the one condemned by God through his many sins, and see such a person—while there are legions of angels appointed to help human nature—pitied by no one.

For each of the angels, seeing that the one who condemned is God, that the one turned away from is the Creator, and that the nature of the sins is such that the good God was compelled—so to speak—to bring the vote against the sinner, each of those who see does not spare, does not look gloomy, does not pity, does not come back so as to plead concerning peace toward such a one.

So let this Jerusalem (for so it will be said according to the letter) have sinned against my Jesus and done such things that Jesus says about her: 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing.' (Matthew 23:37 …)

'Look—your house is left to you.' Let this Jerusalem be left as she has been left. Let the angels who always help Jerusalem—through whom Moses' law also was arranged, 'arranged through angels by the hand of a mediator'—leave Jerusalem and say: her sins have become great; they killed Jesus; they laid hands on the Christ.

As long as the sins were still smaller, we could still plead and intercede about them; we could spare Jerusalem. Who will spare for this? 'If a man sinning sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?' 'Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become a shaking.' And it is said to this one first: 'Who will spare you, Jerusalem? And who will look gloomy over you?' We do not look gloomy over Jerusalem and her disasters and what has happened to that whole people—for by their trespass our salvation has come, to provoke them to jealousy.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why the threat 'Who will spare you?' is spoken to Jerusalem.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To go backward is to remember the things behind as Lot's wife did, so whoever has left sin must not turn back to it or stand in the country around it, but be saved on the mountain, who is the Lord Jesus.
comments.comment:
And to either interpretation of Jerusalem the next words also fit: 'You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You will go backward.' (Jeremiah 15:6) That you have turned away from the Son of God, and through turning away from the Son of God have turned away from God—what need is there even to say it? And since the Jerusalem in Judea turned away from the Christ—from which all the Jews are to be understood—therefore 'You will go backward.' For there was a time when she did not go backward but forward; but now she goes backward, 'and they turned in their hearts toward Egypt' (Acts 7:39)—clearly so that they might go backward. Concerning what 'You will go backward' is, or what it is to stretch forward to the things ahead, we will set it out like this.

The righteous stretches forward to the things ahead, forgetting the things behind. Clearly the one disposed contrary to the righteous remembers the things behind and does not stretch forward to the things ahead. Remembering the things behind, he disobeys Jesus teaching and saying, 'Let him not turn back to take his cloak' (Matthew 24:18); he disobeys Jesus saying, 'Remember Lot's wife'; he disobeys Jesus saying, 'No one who puts hand to the plow and turns back is fit for the kingdom of God.' (Luke 9:62) And in the law it is written that the angels said to Lot who had gone out from Sodom: 'Do not look back, and do not stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be taken along.' And this also has a sense worthy of an angelic spirit: 'Do not look back'—always stretch forward to the things ahead. You have left Sodom; do not turn toward Sodom. You have left wickedness and sin; do not turn back to it, 'and do not stand in all the surrounding country.' Even if you keep the former command that says, 'Do not look back,' it is not enough for you to be saved unless you also hear the second command that says, 'And do not stand in all the surrounding country.' For one who has begun to progress must not stand in the country around Sodom, even if he has crossed Sodom, but having crossed from standing in the surrounding country he must be saved onto the mountain, according to 'Do not look back and do not stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be taken along.' If you want not to be taken along with the people of Sodom, never turn back, and do not stand in the country around Sodom, and be nowhere else than on the mountain—for only there is it possible to be saved.

And the mountain is the Lord Jesus …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to 'go backward' in terms any reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah is a physician sent to a sick people, and those who ought to have listened accuse him in court, so he cries 'Woe is me, mother.'
comments.comment: That people then was sick; there were various diseases in the people who had called upon God. God sent them physicians, the prophets. One of the physicians was also Jeremiah; he convicted those who were sinning, wanting to turn those doing evil. But those who ought to have listened to what was said accused the prophet and accused him before judges like themselves. … And sometimes he says, seeing himself always sued, abused, charged, falsely witnessed against: 'Woe is me, mother, as whom did you bear me?' (Jeremiah 15:10)—he said 'a man' not judging but 'being judged,' and not distinguishing but 'being distinguished throughout all the earth.' (Jeremiah 15:10) And since the sick did not listen to him counseling well and medically, he says: 'I did not benefit.' And since, when he was lending the spiritual silver, those to whom he spoke did not want to listen so as to be benefited from what they heard, he says: 'Nor did anyone owe me, nor did I owe.' (Jeremiah 15:10)
comments.selected_reason: Shows why the prophet laments: his hearers sued the one sent to heal them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The verse is written two ways, 'I did not benefit' and 'I did not owe,' and the first means a teacher is himself helped when his hearers progress.
comments.comment:
For the writing is double: in most copies 'I did not benefit, nor did anyone benefit me,' … but in the most accurate and those agreeing with the Hebrew 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me.' So one must both interpret what is commonly current and carried in the churches and not leave unexplained what is from the Hebrew writings.

He then proclaimed the word; no one received what was said. As a physician also used up the medicines, the sick being undisciplined and filling their own desires.

Perhaps there is a reciprocal affection through the love of humanity of the one benefited toward the one who benefited, so that the speaker also comes to be benefited, since blessed is the one who speaks into ears that hear. … This benefit then a teacher would be benefited from hearers progressing and improving; he would be benefited by having fruit in them. 'No one benefited me.' For if the speaker must have fruit in them, but the hearer receives wrongly and becomes outside what is said, 'No one at all benefited me' is said—since he did not have this benefit which he would have been benefited from the benefited hearer becoming a cause of progress and blessedness for the one who benefited. And otherwise every one who teaches, in the very teaching, as far as the learner is more intelligent, is benefited into what he teaches, into what he learns. For those who speak become better about the lessons they hand over when the hearers, being intelligent and not simply receiving, but cross-examining and asking and testing the will of what is said. So I did not benefit, nor did anyone at all benefit me.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever gives each person what is due can say 'I did not owe,' and 'nor did anyone owe me' means the hearers refused the spiritual money he offered.
comments.comment:
And since another interpretation is also necessary because of the more accurate copies having it thus: 'I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me,' (Jeremiah 15:10) we will interpret the saying having it this way too.

The one who indeed gives back to all their dues—fear to the one due fear, tax to the one due tax, tribute to the one due tribute, honor to the one due honor—and giving back to all what is fitting, so as not to owe what is fitting toward some, having honored parents as parents, so to speak, brothers as brothers, sons as sons, bishops as bishops, elders as elders, deacons as deacons, faithful as faithful, catechumens as catechumens—if he gives back all that is fitting, he did not owe. But if he owes doing what is fitting and has not done it, he cannot say: 'I did not owe'; for owing he did not give back. How then will I also interpret 'nor did anyone owe me'?
