I was lending and wanted to give the spiritual money, but they turned away from what was said and did not present themselves as receptive so as to owe; therefore no one at all owed me. For who received what was said, so that from receiving he might become a debtor of what he heard and be demanded, as a debtor of what was said, for the interest? Better then according to this for the hearer to take logical silver from the speaker and owe than, neither receiving nor taking, not even to owe.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophets boldly rebuked those who sinned, and Jeremiah, having rebuked many and been judged by many, speaks these words of lament.
comments.comment:
From many places one can gather the prophets’ excellences: their freedom, their taut energy, their watchfulness, their being aroused—that when circumstances came they did not worry, because of that freedom, only that they might rebuke, only that they might turn people back, as prophets do when they speak the word of God with boldness, striking those who sin, even if those being rebuked seemed able to do great things.

But even if one can do this from everywhere, let us see it also from what was read today. The prophet rebuked many, and the prophet spoke to many; for he lived among people who had become sinners, as is clear from the captivity that took place in his times. Having rebuked many, and having been judged by many, he utters such words as these (Jeremiah 15:10).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The words 'judged in all the earth' fit the Savior better than the prophet, and 'Woe is me' is not foreign to the Son of God, who said his soul was sorrowful unto death.
comments.comment:
This prophetic word is more properly referred to the Savior. Grant that the prophet says it; yet he will not say it truly, but perhaps by exaggeration—for he was not examined against all the earth. But if I come to my Savior and Lord, and especially because he will come to judgment, and because of the word 'that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged,' (Psalm 51:4) I will see that my Savior and Lord is about to stand before the Father, being judged with all of us humans. And he is judged with all humans. I mean: he is judged, he himself is examined, and he stood defending the truth—not as an accuser. 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth?' (Jeremiah 15:10) A prophet cannot say 'in all the earth.'

But some who love the Lord are also angry and say that the Savior does not speak this, that the voice is not fitting for the Son of God. Yet one must show that 'Woe is me, mother' is not alien to the Son of God: 'My soul is very sorrowful unto death,' (Matthew 26:38) and 'My soul is troubled,' and of the things said in the prophets likewise also here: 'Woe is me, mother, as what man did you bear me—a man judged and examined in all the earth' (Jeremiah 15:10) …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whenever a Christian is judged for being a Christian, it is Christ who is judged in him, so the words 'judged in all the earth' are true of Christ.
comments.comment:
'As whom did you bear me, a man judged and examined in all the earth?' (Jeremiah 15:10) If you see the martyrs everywhere being judged and in each church standing before the judges, you will see how Jesus Christ is judged in each of the martyrs; for he himself is the one judged in those who bear witness to the truth. And you will be persuaded to accept this when you see that he does not say you are in prison when you are in prison, but himself; not you hungry when you are hungry, but himself; not you thirsty, but himself. 'I was in prison and you came to me.

I was hungry and you gave me to eat; I was thirsty and you gave me drink.' So even if a Christian is judged not for something else, not for his own sins, but because he is a Christian, it is Christ who is judged. In all the earth then Christ Jesus is judged; and as often as a Christian is judged, it is Christ who is judged—not only in these lawcourts, but take a Christian to be falsely accused and charged about something: then too Christ is judged unjustly.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear, followable sense to the words 'judged ... in all the earth'.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Savior took up the weakness of our sins and came down to those who curse him, so his strength failed among them.
comments.comment:
'My strength failed among those who curse me.' (Jeremiah 15:10)

The apostle says about the Savior that 'he was crucified from weakness.' (2 Corinthians 13:4) And the prophet says things near these in 'Lord, who believed our report? And to whom was the Lord's arm revealed? We announced before him as a child, as a root in thirsty ground; we saw him, and he had no form or beauty, but his form was without honor, failing beside the sons of humans. A man being in blow and in toil and knowing how to bear weakness, because his face was turned away from dishonor, he was dishonored and not reckoned. This one bears our lawless deeds and is in pain about us, and we reckoned him to be in toil and in blow and in mistreatment. But he was wounded through our lawless deeds, and has been softened through our sins; the discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruise we were healed.' So he took up the weakness of our sins and wore us and came to those who curse him, and his strength failed from those who curse him as he came down from heavens. For at once he took up the form of the slave and emptied himself, as the apostle said that 'he emptied himself, taking a slave's form.' So he says: 'My strength failed among those who curse me.' (Jeremiah 15:10)
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'my strength failed' by Christ's coming in weakness, with Scripture a reader knows.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: In every rational person the strength of the Word either grows or fails, failing in the sinful soul and bearing fruit in the righteous.
comments.comment:
Let us see whether, the Word himself giving, we can also say something clearer than what has been said toward 'My strength failed among those who curse me.' (Jeremiah 15:10) 'There was the true light, which enlightens every human coming into the world.' … 'The true light' is the Son of God, 'which enlightens every human coming into the world.' … And whoever is rational shares in the true light, and every human is rational. So of all humans who share in the Word, in some the strength of the Word has grown, and in some it fails.

If you see a passionate and sinful soul, you will see there the strength of the Word failing; but if you see a holy and righteous soul, you will see the strength of the Word bearing fruit day by day, and you will fit what is said about Jesus to the righteous. For not by himself alone 'did Jesus advance in wisdom and stature and grace with God and humans,' but also in each of those who receive the advance in wisdom, stature, and grace, Jesus advances 'in wisdom, stature, and grace with God and humans.' So the Word, the Son of God, who is in the one saying 'Woe is me, mother' and what follows, says that 'My strength failed among those who curse me.'

Whoever curses the Word at once receives the punishment for cursing the Word, for blaming Jesus' teaching; for Jesus' strength fails in such a one, and there is no strength of Word in him. And again from the contrary: if you bless Jesus and accept him, his strength suffers the opposite of what it suffered among those who curse. For as there it failed among those who curse, so here it grows among those who bless.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Savior owed nothing, for the ruler of this world had nothing in him, and no one owed him because he forgave all their debts.
comments.comment:
'I owed nothing, and no one owed me.' … 'The ruler of this world comes, and he has nothing in me.' (John 14:30) And truly he owed nothing. But each of us is a debtor by sins and a debtor holding a certificate of debt. After his certificate has been wiped out, how many certificates have they made again? 'He who did no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth,' … made no certificate of debt.

And what of 'no one owed me'? How shall we explain this of the Savior—'no one owed me'? Even if we have read it this way, we must also know that most copies of the Seventy’s edition do not have it so; later, when we examined the remaining editions as well, we learned that it is a scribal error. And yet—'not even one' to me. So that not even one owed him anything: he forgave all their debts. 'A certain creditor had two debtors; one owed five hundred denarii, and the other fifty. When they had nothing to repay, he forgave them both. … These things because of 'I owed nothing, and no one owed me,' which it was necessary to set before you. 'I owed nothing, and no one owed me; my strength failed among those who curse me.' Even if he died 'from weakness, yet he lives from the power of God.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The speaker asks that his strength may come when those who speak ill of him are guided, and says that the Savior stood before the Father for them in the time of their evils.
comments.comment: 'May it be, Lord, when they are guided; if I did not stand before you in the time of their evils.' (Jeremiah 15:11) What is 'May it be, Lord'? Let the one able gather such a thing from himself. 'Master Lord, when they are guided'—may the strength that fails among those who curse come to be, when, having repented after speaking ill of me, they turn to the straight way and travel it. 'May it be, Master, when they are guided; if I did not stand before you.' (1 John 2:2) Then he justifies himself about those who speak ill of him saying: 'If I did not stand before you in the time of their evils.' He stood before the Father as 'atonement for our sins' and pleaded about them in that very time of our evils. For he did not stand after the time of our evils, but 'while we were still sinners Christ died for us'—'if I did not stand before you in the time of their evils, in the time of their afflictions, for good against the enemy.' And in the time of their affliction, he says, the one toward the enemy, I stood before you for them. And who is the enemy but 'our adversary the devil,' who afflicted us? And clearly in the time of that enmity against humans our Savior stood before the Father and begged about our captivity, that we might be redeemed and delivered from the enemy. Let the Savior or the prophet have said these things; for the prophet too can have said such things and prayed about the people in 'the time of their evils.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: 'Not unto long-suffering' asks God to be long-suffering no more over what was dared against the speaker, and after the passion God showed it no more toward the people.
comments.comment:
'And I will enslave you among all your enemies in the land which you did not know.' (Jeremiah 15:14) That people has been enslaved among the enemies, and has come to be in the land which they did not know. 'For a fire has been kindled from my wrath; it will burn upon you.' (Jeremiah 15:14)

After these things and the words of the threats spoken toward the people, the one who prayed above completes the prayer and joins to what was said beforehand these things: 'You know, Lord; remember me and visit me, and acquit me from those who pursue me—not unto long-suffering.' (Jeremiah 15:15) And let the prophet say these things, pursued by those who were convicted, hated by those who do not make room for the truth; for he became an enemy to those who hear, speaking truly to them. And let our Savior also say the same, who was also pursued by the people and says: 'Not unto long-suffering.' … What is 'not unto long-suffering'? You were always long-suffering toward the people upon their sins, but upon the things dared against me do not be long-suffering. And truly God was not long-suffering.

If you examine the times of the passion and of Jerusalem's fall and of the city's demolition, and how God abandoned that people since they killed the Christ, you will see that he no longer used long-suffering toward the people. And if you want, hear: from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar until the demolition of the temple forty-two years were completed. For some short time had to be granted for repentance, especially because of those from the people who were going to believe from the signs and wonders that would come to be through the apostles.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the unusual words 'not unto long-suffering' and how Jerusalem's fall is read in them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet is reproached by those who set aside God's words, and whoever wants a portion with the prophets must be ready to suffer what they suffered.
comments.comment:
'Know that I received reproach concerning you from those who set aside your words.' (Jeremiah 15:15) Let the prophet, speaking and made nothing of for what he said, be set aside by sinners; for he himself says: 'I continued being mocked.' So he was reproached by those who set aside the words spoken through him by God, and he prays, upon being reproached, to be helped by God saying: 'Know that I received reproach concerning you from those who set aside your words; finish them.' (Jeremiah 15:15) Let the prophet say it, but 'finish them' spoken by the Savior fits better; for a finishing came upon Jerusalem and the people, upon what happened from the people's plot against our Savior.

After these things it is necessary—because the prophets suffered much convicting and ambassadoring the word and taking what was commanded by God—to remind the hearers about their life and their promises and our choice, so that as far as we can, if we want to have rest with the prophets, we may zealously imitate the prophets' works.

What I mean is like this: often in prayers we say: Almighty God, give our portion with the prophets, give our portion with the apostles of your Christ, that we may also be found with Christ himself. And saying these things we do not perceive what we pray; for in effect we say this: grant us to suffer what the prophets suffered, grant us also to be hated as the prophets were hated, give such words for which we will be hated, grant us to fall into as many circumstances as the apostles. For to say 'give me a portion with the prophets' while neither having suffered the prophets' things nor wanting to suffer is unjust. To say 'give me a portion with the apostles' while not wanting from Paul's disposition, speaking truly, to say: 'In toils more abundantly, in blows more abundantly, in prisons beyond measure, in deaths often' and what follows, is most unjust of all. If then we want to come to be with the prophets, look at the prophets' lives—that from convicting, from rebuking, from striking they were judged, examined, condemned. 'They were stoned, they were sawn, they were tested, they died by murder of sword, they went about in sheepskins, in goatskins, lacking, afflicted, mistreated, wandering upon deserts' (Hebrews 11:37–38)—when there were many synagogues of Jews; and these were 'wandering upon deserts and mountains and caves and the holes of the earth. … What then is strange if someone wanting to zealously imitate the prophetic life, convicting, striking the one who sins, is spoken ill of, hated, plotted against? … The marvelous apostles, insulted countless times because of the truth, say: 'I am well pleased in weaknesses, in insults and necessities, in persecutions and distresses, for Christ.' Only may I, being insulted, know that I am insulted for no other reason than for Christ; coming into necessities, know that the ground of the necessities is Christ. May I, being abused, know that the pretext of the abuse is no other than that I vindicate the truth and ambassador for what is written, so that according to God's word everything may come to be—for this reason I am blasphemed. So let us all too, as much strength as there is, hasten upon the prophetic life, upon the apostolic life, not fleeing what is burdensome; for if an athlete flees the burdensome of the contest, he will not receive the pleasant of the crown.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the reproach in the verse and what it means to ask for a share with the prophets.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet's joy in God's word is still to come, and he refused to sit in a council of those playing rather than those serious, choosing to be God's friend.
comments.comment:
'And your word will be to me for gladness.' (Jeremiah 15:16) It is not now, but 'it will be'; for upon the present your word is to me for imprisonments, for lawsuits, for affairs, for ill repute, for toils, but the end of these will be gladness. 'And your word will be to me for gladness and joy of my heart, because your name has been called upon me, Lord Almighty.' (Jeremiah 15:16) Even if Christ says it, the Father's name has been called upon him.

'I did not sit in their council of those playing.' (Jeremiah 15:17) If ever the prophet saw the council not of those serious but of those playing, he fled rather gathering than hastened upon a synagogue of those playing. So you must understand a difference between a council of those playing and of those serious. This council is serious and does everything with seriousness and things worthy of seriousness and according to what is said: seriousness is the word, seriousness is the life, and everywhere the council is not of those playing but of those serious.

But when the council, leaving the seriousness about what is necessary, has leisure for the games of this age and games from wickedness, it becomes a council of those playing. So this one says: 'I did not sit in their council of those playing, but I was cautious from before your hand.' (Jeremiah 15:17) Two things being set before me—to sit in a council of those playing and to stumble against you God and not please you, or to rise from a council of those playing and do the things that were dear to you—I chose rather to stand up from the council of those playing and be a friend to you than, doing the contrary, to become an enemy to your blessedness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'council of those playing' means and why the prophet's gladness lies ahead.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To sit alone is to live so unlike the many that no one imitates you, and to be filled with bitternesses is to eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth with its bitter herbs, as Paul did.
comments.comment:
'I was sitting alone.' And the words are managed here. Whenever there is a multitude of sinners and they do not bear the righteous living righteously, it is not out of place for one fleeing the council of wickedness to imitate the one who said: 'I was sitting alone,' to imitate also Elijah who says: 'Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I alone have been left, and they seek my soul to take it.' (1 Kings 19:10, 14) And perhaps even if you examine more deeply 'I was sitting alone,' you will find some mind worthy of prophetic depth. Whenever we imitate the life of the many, so as not to be withdrawn and better and exceptional beside the many, I cannot say: 'I was sitting alone,' but: I was sitting with many.

But when my life becomes hard to imitate, so that I become so great that no one is near me in character, in word, in deeds, in wisdom, then I can say—because of being alone such and no one imitating me—'I was sitting alone.'

So it is possible even if you are not an elder and not a bishop and not honored with some church honor to say this, to zealously imitate 'I was sitting alone' and take up a life so as to say: 'I was sitting alone.' 'Because I was filled with bitternesses.' (Jeremiah 15:17) If 'narrow and afflicted is the way,' how does your feast come to be with bitter herbs? For when you feast, it says 'you shall eat unleavened breads upon bitter herbs.' (Exodus 12:8; Num 9:11) What the word wants saying that the one feasting to God must eat 'unleavened breads upon bitter herbs' (1 Corinthians 5:8) must be considered. The apostle interpreted the unleavened breads; the interpretation is not mine; but what follows of the interpretation must necessarily be near the apostolic interpretation.

The apostle interpreted the things about the unleavened breads saying: 'Let us feast not in old leaven nor in leaven of wickedness and evil, but in unleavened breads of sincerity and truth.' (1 Corinthians 5:8) It is necessary to give the account about the bitter herbs following upon the unleavened breads being of sincerity and truth. Have sincerity and truth, and bitter herbs will be yours, and you eat with bitter herbs the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth—as Paul. Since he ate the unleavened breads of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? Saying 'I have become your enemy speaking truly to you.' How did he eat bitter herbs? 'In toil and labor, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, apart from the things besides.' (2 Corinthians 11:27–28)

So the law said: 'You shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs'; and it did not say: you shall eat unleavened breads with bitter herbs until you are filled, as upon certain other things it has been said: 'You shall eat and be filled.' But the prophet presses further saying that I did not eat bitterness, but 'I was filled with bitternesses'; as much strength as there was I partook of bitter affairs, so as to partake with the fullest bitter herbs.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah was embittered by what he suffered from his hearers and by the impiety he saw, yet could not decline the ministry.
comments.comment: “I was sitting alone, because I was filled with bitterness” (Jeremiah 15:17) and what follows; for he [Jeremiah] was petitioning for them, and they were plotting, and yet it was not possible to decline the ministry. He was being embittered, then, both suffering from them and suffering-with those suffering and being weighed down beyond measure at those being impious (Jeremiah 15:17).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who grieved the prophet overpowered him in this world because the kingdom of God is not from this age, as the martyrs show.
comments.comment: 'Why do those who hate me overpower?' (Jeremiah 15:18) He had many affairs; he suffered from those not wanting to hear what is true, and those were more powerful than him here in this age, since the kingdom of God is not from this age but from the better places, as the Savior says: 'If my kingdom were from this world, my servants would have fought, that I not be handed over to the Jews.' So those grieving the prophet overpowered him in this world. That they are strong—look at the martyrs. The judge sits judging and living luxuriously in the lawcourt; the Christian, in whom Christ is being judged, was filled with bitternesses and has been overpowered by the unjust and is condemned.
comments.selected_reason: Answers the prophet's question in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whether spoken by the prophet, by the righteous or by the Savior, 'my wound is hard' is followed by healing, because the wound does not remain but passes.
comments.comment: 'My wound is hard; from where will I be healed?' (Jeremiah 15:18) Those who overpower me strike me, and my wound is hard. Whether he prophesies the Lord's cross (for the cross is a hard wound, as far as it lies with those who crucify him), or whether it is said about all the righteous in whom he receives a hard wound, or even if you hear this upon the prophet (for he too suffered the things written in the prophecy), it admits the same sense according to the wording that says: 'My wound is hard.' 'From where will I be healed?' Even if the Savior says: 'From where will I be healed?' he prophesies the resurrection from the dead after the hard wound; and even if it is taken upon the righteous, after the wounds healing comes again. 'Coming to be it became for me as false water, not having faith'; for the wound does not remain but passes.
comments.selected_reason: Reads the wound and its healing in a way that a reader can follow.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: To restore is to put someone back into what is his own, like a dislocated limb set right or an exile returned to his fatherland, so God promises to restore those who turn back.
comments.comment:
'Therefore thus says the Lord: If you turn, I will also restore you.' These things are said again toward each whom God will call to turn toward him. And a mystery seems to me to be announced here in the 'I will restore you.' No one is restored into some place never having been there at all, but restoration is into what is one's own. For example if a limb of mine becomes dislocated, the physician tries to make a restoration of the dislocation.

Whenever someone comes to be outside the fatherland, whether justly or unjustly, and then receives again the power to be in the fatherland according to the laws, he was restored upon his own fatherland. Think the same with me also upon a soldier cast out from his own battle-line and being restored. So here he says toward us who turned away that, if we turn, he will restore us. For the end of the promise is also such, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles in the 'until times of restoration of all things which God spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets from of old' (Acts 3:21) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'I will restore you' means with plain pictures.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Even those blessed through later good works must first receive the repayment of their sins, because a just God gives neither the better without the worse nor the worse without the better.
comments.comment:
So that those who were fished and afterward came into the mountains may not suppose that these things have come to them from righteousness, the word reminds not only them but also us of the former sins. Therefore after the benefits it is said: 'And their injustices were not hidden before my eyes.' … What follows is about to put a contest before us. For if we understand it as following, we will take careful thought about the repayment of the sins; and if it seems not to follow what was set out before about those being fished and hunted, even so it throws us into no small contest. For he says: 'And I will repay first double their injustices and their sins, with which they profaned my land in the carcasses of the abominations and by their lawless deeds with which they filled my inheritance.' (Jeremiah 16:18) Whether some, not understanding, removed the 'first' from what is written, or the Seventy managed to remove it, God would know. But we, comparing with the remaining editions, found it lying there: 'And I will repay first double their injustices,' (Jeremiah 16:18) so that it may be shown that even if through their second works they were worthy of blessedness, since they are humans and have come to be in sins, they must first receive their sins.

And see whether the word is not true. Who will not receive the sins—except the one who, after believing and receiving forgiveness of sins (so as to hear Jesus say: 'Your sins are forgiven you'), no longer sins? But if after the forgiveness of sins and the economy of the washing of regeneration we sin—as we the many do, who have not been perfected like the apostles—and after sinning, and while sinning, also do some things that are due, what awaits us must be considered. If we leave life holding sins and also holding brave deeds, will we be saved through the brave deeds and released concerning the things we sinned in knowledge? Or will we be punished through the sins and nowhere receive a wage for the brave deeds? But neither the one—I mean receiving the worse and not receiving the better—is according to the just God, nor the other—I mean receiving the better and not receiving the worse—is according to the just God, who wants to cleanse and cut out the wickedness.

For grant that you have built, after the foundation Christ Jesus whom you were taught, not only gold and silver and precious stone—if indeed you have gold, much gold or little; grant that you have silver, precious stone; but not only these, I say—grant that you also have wood and hay and straw. What do you wish to happen to you after departure? Either to enter into the holy things with your wood and with your hay and straw, so as to defile the kingdom of God? Or again do you wish to remain because of the hay, the wood, the straw in the fire and receive nothing for the gold and silver and precious stone? This too is not reasonable.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'first double' and why sins are repaid before the good works are rewarded.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The nations come from the end of the earth, meaning the last of humanity, the foolish, ignoble and despised, and say that their fathers' idols are false and give no profit.
comments.comment:
'Lord, my strength and my help and my refuge in a day of evils; to you nations will come from the end of the earth and will say: How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no profit in them.' (Jeremiah 16:19) From the end of the earth the nations came to God, and the nations have said: 'How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no profit in them.'

How 'from the end of the earth'? There are some who are first of the earth, and there are some who are last of the earth. Who are first? 'The wise of the world' are first of the earth—not simply first, but 'the wise of the world, the well-born,' the rich, those in office. Who are last? 'God chose the foolish things of the world, the ignoble, the despised, the things that are not.' Therefore 'nations will come from the end of the earth,' as if he said: from the last of the humans upon the earth, from the foolish, from the ignoble, from the despised, 'and they will say: How false were the idols our fathers acquired, and there is no profit in them.' Not that there are some true idols, against which the false are spoken by contrast, but idols which by nature are false—'and there is no profit in them.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains 'from the end of the earth' and the confession of the nations.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Men make gods for themselves not only from statues but from molded doctrines of the mind, and God will show them his hand and his power at the time of the Lord's presence.
comments.comment:
'If a man will make gods for himself.' (Jeremiah 16:20) Not only from statues do men make gods for themselves, but you will also find them making gods for themselves from moldings of the mind. For as many as can mold another god and another world-making besides the one written up by the Spirit—a management of the world besides the true world—all these have made gods for themselves and have worshiped the works of their hands. Consider, for example, among the Greeks those who generated doctrines of this philosophy or that, or among the heresies those who first generated doctrines: these made idols for themselves and moldings of the soul, and turning they worshiped the works of their hands, accepting their own moldings as truth.

Therefore the word, refuting all who make gods for themselves both sensibly and intelligibly, says: 'If a man will make gods for himself—and these are not gods? For this reason I will show them my hand at this time, and I will make known to them also my power.' At what time, if not this one—pointing to the time of the Lord’s presence? 'And they will know,' he says, 'that my name is Lord.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to make gods for oneself beyond carved idols.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen and an adamant point on the heart, because each sin we commit leaves an imprint in us that cannot be wiped away like ink.
comments.comment:
Then there is another prophecy, which somehow we did not find among the Seventy, but we found in the remaining editions—clearly lying in the Hebrew—and it is filled with most necessary matters that can, if we pay attention, turn our soul back. The words run thus: 'The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved with an adamant point upon the breast of their heart.' (Jeremiah 17:1)

It is easier to give oneself over and say: These things are written about the Jews, that their sin 'is written.' But if you see, as we have often shown, Judah spoken tropically as Christ, perhaps 'the sin of Judah' is ours—of those who believe upon Christ who is from the tribe of Judah. And if you can also hear it more mystically another way, perhaps it prophesies about Judas who handed him over, so that the prophecy about him says: 'The sin of Judah is written with an iron pen, engraved with an adamant point upon the breast of the heart.' … But again 'their' does not follow for that one. Perhaps then he was speaking upon us: if we become sinners, these prophesied things reach us.

We have sinned, and our sin is not written outside us, but in our heart, and it is written 'with an iron pen, with an adamant point.' (Jeremiah 17:1) That the sins we commit are inscribed into us by the sinning, the matter itself will show. I did not know this deed or this sin in myself; having done it I have its imprint, and as it were the imprint of my committed sin has been written in my soul. And if my sin had been written with ink, I would have wiped it away; but now it is written 'with an iron pen,' written 'with an adamant point,' written 'upon the breast of our heart,' so that I may come to the place of teaching and the prophecy that says may be fulfilled: 'Nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest, and nothing covered that will not be revealed.' … My breast was stripped bare, and the heart holding the written letters of the sin—'with the pen upon my breast and in my heart the imprints of my sins.' For 'nothing is hidden that will not be made manifest.' …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what it means that sin is engraved on the heart.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The curse falls on those who suppose the Savior was merely a man, and on whoever strengthens the flesh of his arm or trusts in the dignities of friends, since our hope is upon our Lord, who is Christ Jesus.
comments.comment:
… 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' (Jeremiah 17:5) From those who suppose that the Son of God, the Savior, was merely a man—for they dared, along with many human evils, to say also this, that there is no God who is 'the only-begotten,' 'the firstborn of all creation'—'cursed' is 'the one who has his hope upon a man.' It is clear that those who have their hope upon a man are under a curse.

I would say that I do not have my hope upon a man. Hoping upon Christ Jesus, I do not know a man. Not only do I not know a man, but I know Wisdom, absolute Righteousness, the one through whom 'all things were created' among the authorities. 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' (Jeremiah 17:5) Even if the Savior bears witness that what he wore was a man—yet even if he was a man, now he is in no way a man. For 'if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet we know him so no longer,' (2 Corinthians 5:16) says the apostle. Through him I am no longer a man, if I follow his words; but he says: 'I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.' Therefore, as he is 'firstborn from the dead,' so he has become firstborn of all humans by changing them toward God.

'Cursed,' then, 'is the man who has his hope upon a man, and will strengthen the flesh of his arm'—whoever ratifies the fleshly things, whoever acquires bodily strength and campaigns according to the flesh. But the holy one is not like that: for 'he does not strengthen the flesh of his arm,' for he 'always' has 'the dying of Jesus in his body,' and he puts to death 'the members that are upon the earth—fornication, uncleanness.' Having put these to death, 'he does not strengthen the flesh of his arm.'

'Cursed is the one who has his hope upon a man.' And at the same time this is said toward those who hope in dignities. So-and-so is my friend; he is a centurion, he is a steward; so-and-so is my friend and is rich and supplies me. Then toward such a person also this is said: 'Cursed is the man who has his hope upon a man.' We hope upon no human being, even if they seem to be our friends; for we do not hope upon them but upon our Lord, who is Christ Jesus …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what hoping upon a man means and applies it plainly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The partridge is a crafty, deceitful and unclean animal, so it cannot be ranked with the Savior and must be tested as a figure of the opposing one.
comments.comment:
We have come upon the much-discussed question, to see what the partridge is, concerning which Scripture now says: 'A partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear, making its wealth not with judgment. In the middle of its days they will abandon it, and at its end it will be a fool.' (Jeremiah 17:11)

From the account of the natures of animals we must take up what has been recorded about the partridge, so that knowing the things about the animal we may know whether the partridge now spoken of must be ranked upon a better or upon a worse. It is said to be a most ill-natured animal, and deceitful, and thoroughly crafty, wanting to deceive those who hunt it, and often rolling about the feet of the hunter so as to distract him—as if the animal were near—so that he may not come upon the nest. And whenever it judges that it has distracted the hunter and the nestlings have fled, then it too flies away. And the animal is utterly unclean, so that the males fight one another over mating and male mounts male.

If then this animal is ill-natured and unclean and thoroughly crafty and deceitful, it is clear that to rank it upon a better and to say it can be referred to the Savior appears impious. Therefore we must see, if we wish to interpret it of the opposing one, whether the whole interpretation follows for us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The partridge gathers what it did not bear, because the devil gathers another's creatures and makes them his own, growing rich without judgment by deceiving the simple.
comments.comment:
Let us begin from: 'A partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear.' (Jeremiah 17:11) Therefore the devil does not gather his own creatures; he does not gather what he begot; but when he calls, he gathers another’s creatures and makes them his own. A partridge called through Valentinus; a partridge called through Marcion; it called through Basilides, through all the heterodox. For none of those could speak the voice of Jesus: 'My sheep will hear my voice.' But the voice of Jesus is in Paul and Peter; therefore Paul said: 'Do you seek a proof of Christ who speaks in me?' (2 Corinthians 13:3)

But the voice of the partridge that gathered what it did not bear is in those who lead astray and deceive, through their simplicity and lack of preparation, the simpler among the believers. Therefore 'a partridge called; it gathered what it did not bear, making its wealth not with judgment.' The partridge grew rich. See how many myriads are his; many have become the partridge’s—of the opposing power. And he made his wealth not caring about judgment and not having judgment, but acting without judgment. Therefore it is said that the partridge is 'making its wealth not with judgment.' But my Savior makes his wealth with judgment, and his wealth is judged and chosen.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's picture of the partridge gathering what it did not bear.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those once called by the partridge abandon him in the middle of his days, since Christ drew them out of this age, and at his end he is a fool though he was once wise.
comments.comment:
'And in the middle of his days they will abandon him.' (Jeremiah 17:11) We all who once came under the calling partridge—for he called not only through those named before, but also through all who simply deceive and, as if unto piety, summon godlessness unto doctrines contrary to the truth—but 'in the middle of his days' (Jeremiah 17:11) we have abandoned him. For all his days are the days of this age; but since Christ Jesus drew us out of the present evil age, therefore 'in the middle of his days' we have abandoned him.

'And at his end he will be a fool.' For when was he wise, that at his end he should become a fool? But we will say that he was wise; for 'the serpent was the wisest of all the beasts of the earth which the Lord God made.' (Genesis 3:1) …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the middle of his days' and 'a fool at his end' mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who have turned away from the divine spring are written on the earth, enrolled with a citizenship below, while the names of the disciples are written in the heavens by the quality of their lives.
comments.comment: … and again in Jeremiah it is said: 'having turned away to the earth they have written' (Jer 17:13). Those having turned away from the divine spring are written of, being enrolled in the earth, as having the citizenship below and bearing 'the image of the jar' (cf. 1 Corinthians 15:49). But of the disciples, 'the names are written in the heavens' (Luke 10:20). He does not speak of these designations by combining letters, but of the very qualities which signify them, for the definition of a name is given thus: a name is a principal designation representing the quality of the one named. This is the descriptive name: man, heaven. 'Is written,' therefore, that is, has been arranged. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who always follows Jesus does not grow weary, since the following itself takes away the labor, and he desires the day of the resurrection of the holy ones rather than a human day of longer life.
comments.comment:
'Behold, they say to me: Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come. But I did not grow weary following after you.' (Jeremiah 17:16) Jesus says to you: 'Take up your cross and follow me,' and 'Leave all things and follow me,' and 'Whoever does not leave father and mother and follow after me is not worthy to be my disciple.' (Matthew 10:37-38) If then you become such that you always follow Jesus, you will also follow, and as long as you follow you will not grow weary; for 'there will be no toil in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel.' (Numbers 23:21) There is no labor for the one following Jesus; the very following takes away the labor.

Therefore he himself says, so that we may no longer grow weary—having grown weary before we began to follow him: 'Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest.' (Matthew 11:28) If then, laboring, we come to him and follow him, we will say: 'But I did not grow weary following after you.'

And it is consequent for us to say also: 'I did not desire a human day.' There is a day of a human, and there is a day of God. Let each of us desire the day of the resurrection of the holy ones, not that day concerning which it is written: 'Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; and this is darkness and not light.' Who is the one who says: 'And I did not desire a human day'? The clarity of the word will convict us that we have desired a human day. Often when we have fallen sick and come into a fantasy of death, at the departure we beg the brothers who watch over us and say: Ask for me a leave, ask for me to remain in life. Saying these things we do not desire a holy day of God, but a human day. Therefore putting away love of the body and the desire for a human day, let us seek to see that day in which we will obtain the blessedness in Christ Jesus …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prophet's words about following without weariness and not desiring a human day.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah is told to go down to the potter's house because a hearer of the word is taught either higher things by going up, as Moses did, or lower things by going down.
comments.comment:
… 'The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down into the house of the potter.' (Jeremiah 18:2) Jeremiah is above; he has gone up beyond the clay vessels. Below are the clay vessels, and the nature that administers the clay vessels, going down with those administered, is below. Therefore the word spoken to Jeremiah from the Lord says to him: 'Arise and go down into the house of the potter, and there you will hear my words.' (Jeremiah 18:2)

To Moses it is said: 'Go up into the mountain and hear'; to Jeremiah: 'Go down into the house of the potter and hear.' (Jeremiah 18:2) For each of those who hear a word is either taught about the things higher up or learns about the things lower down. If I am taught the lower things, I go down by the word in order to see the lower things; if I learn the higher things, I go up by the word upon the higher things in order to behold what is there. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet is told to go down and hear.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A vessel of clay that has room for repentance can be remolded, but when it settles into a state that can hardly be changed it becomes a shard and is cast away.
comments.comment: … it is commanded "to go down into the house of the potter, and having gone down" (Jeremiah 18:2) he saw a "vessel" being flattened, "clay" being shaped into a "vessel"; and since the dwelling did not have the form of the "vessel" of "honor", "it fell from his hands"; the potter "let it fall" so that it might be remolded by the potter. Therefore, when a place has capacity for repentance, it is a clay "vessel" capable of being remolded, of being transformed. But when it has reached a stability in a state almost unchangeable or difficult to change, then it is henceforth a "shard". For this reason it is cast away. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: On the simpler reading, the clay vessel that fell from the potter's hands and was made again shows that God, the potter of our bodies, can take them up again when they fall apart and make them better.
comments.comment: 'And a word of the Lord came to me, saying: If as the potter I will not be able to do to you, house of Israel? says the Lord.' … Some considered these things more simply and understood. I will set their account and narration before you; after these things, if we have something deeper, we will narrate that too. Here, they say, the things about the resurrection can be shown. For if the clay vessel fell apart from the potter’s hands and from the same matter of the same clay he makes 'it another vessel as it was pleasing before him,' (Jeremiah 18:4) the potter God of our bodies, the craftsman of our construction, when this falls apart and is crushed for whatever cause, can take it up again and renew it and make it a more beautiful and better 'other vessel as it was pleasing before him to make.' …
comments.selected_reason: Gives a plain reading of the potter and the reshaped vessel.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: When God wants to give good hope, he shows the prophet a clay vessel that falls apart in the potter's hands and is reshaped, so he can set Israel right.
comments.comment: … But when He wants to hold out good hopes to them, He brings the prophet down to a potter's workshop. He does not show him an earthen vessel; He shows him a clay vessel taking shape in the potter's hands, falling apart, and then He adds, 'If this potter takes up the vessel that fell apart and reshapes it, will I not be far more able to set you right after you have fallen apart?' (Jeremiah 18:3-6). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet is shown a clay vessel and what it promises.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Since the end spoken against a nation or kingdom depends on whether it turns or sins, the saying that God repents needs a defense, because repenting seems unworthy of a wise God who foreknows.
comments.comment:
'At the end I will speak upon a nation or also upon a kingdom.' … It will seem that the end has been spoken simply. But such a thing has been said. In 'I will speak upon a nation or kingdom,' (Jeremiah 18:7) the end is of this sort: 'I will tear down' is said as the end to the former nation; to the second: 'I will rebuild you.' And again 'I will uproot' is said to the former, and 'I will plant' to the second. Since then the end has been spoken, must the end come to be? God who does not repent is said according to Scripture to repent. And let us attend to the wording, that if we can make a defense how these things are said, we may accept the word.

'At the end I will speak,' he says, 'upon a nation or upon a kingdom to lift them away and destroy; and if that nation turns from their evils of which I spoke upon it, I will also repent concerning the evils which I planned to do to them. And at the end I will speak upon a nation or upon a kingdom to be built up and planted; and they will do the evil things before me so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the goods which I spoke to do to them.' … Concerning the repentance of God we are required to make a defense; for it seems blameworthy and unworthy not only of God but even of the wise man to repent. For I do not conceive a wise man repenting; but the one who repents, as far as the custom of the word goes, repents over not having planned well. But God, being foreknower of the things to come, cannot have planned badly and for that reason repent. How then did Scripture introduce him saying 'I will repent'—and in the Kingdoms: 'I have regretted that I anointed Saul as king,' (1 Samuel 15:11) and generally: 'and repenting over the evils'? …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is said to repent because, when his economy is intertwined with human affairs, he speaks as one speaks to infants, who cannot be made to understand any other way.
comments.comment:
… But see what we are taught generally about God. On the one hand: 'God is not as a man to be deceived, nor as a son of man to be threatened,' and we learn that God is not as a man; and through another wording that God is as a man, when his economy is intertwined with human affairs. For 'of his greatness there will be no end,' and countless other things from the holy writings fit 'God is not as a man.' But when the divine economy is intertwined with human affairs, it bears the human mind and manner and wording.

And just as we, if we converse with a two-year-old child, babble because of the child—for keeping the dignity of perfect adult age without coming down to their dialect we cannot make the children understand—conceive something such also about God, whenever he manages the race of humans, and especially those still infants. See how we perfect men also change the names toward infants. Are we then imperfect? Or is it granted that one speaking to a child by accommodation speak a child’s dialect? And God indeed speaks to children; 'Behold,' says the Savior also, 'I and the children whom God has given me.' So then conceive also the Scripture saying: 'The Lord your God bore your manners, as if a man should bear the manners of his son.' Since then we repent, whenever God converses with us who repent he says: I repent; and threatening us he does not pretend to be a foreknower, but as speaking to infants he threatens.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why Scripture says God repents.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the evils God says he fashions are in his hand, they can fall away from it, so that he may change them and do good.
comments.comment: Next after the word about the two nations—the former to which the threat is given, and the second to which the promise is given—he says (clearly he spoke to the former): 'And now I said to men of Judah and to those inhabiting Jerusalem: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I fashion evils upon you.' (Jeremiah 18:11) Because these things which I fashion upon you are in my hand, they can fall away. Make these things fall away from my hand, that I may change the evils which I fashion upon you and do goods. …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Those who are called to repent and answer that they will go behind their turnings-away, doing what pleases an evil heart, show by sinful lives what they say, and the fearful things Israel did are measured against those who turned to the Lord and believed.
comments.comment:
'Let each turn from his evil way, and make your practices better.' (Jeremiah 18:11) Sometimes the more simple say: Blessed are the older humans, because they heard the Lord through the prophet saying: 'And the Lord spoke to them.' And now the Lord says also to us through the things written: 'Let each turn from his evil way'; the Lord himself converses with you saying: 'And make your practices better.'

But these answered to whom the exhortative words about repentance were spoken, and let us see what they answered, that we too may not answer such things. What then answering do they say? 'We will take courage, that we will go behind our turnings-away, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart.' … And if you do not say it in words, but your life is such as to sin, you also say by force through the evil deeds after the exhortative words: 'We will take courage…'

And what is 'we will go behind our turnings-away'? Those who began to put the hand to the plow and those being taught turned away from the base things. Whenever then someone putting the hand to the plow turns to the things behind, he will go 'behind his turnings-away'; for he will go behind those things from which he turned away, and he runs back upon those sins which he left. And of those hearing these things, whether catechumens who left the gentile life or faithful already advanced in stretching forward to the things ahead, if the life has become wretched, they say nothing other than: 'We will go behind our turnings-away, and each will do the pleasing things of his evil heart.' For there is an evil heart and there is a good heart. Therefore let no one go 'behind his turnings-away' nor do 'the pleasing things of his evil heart.'

'Therefore,' toward those answering these things, 'says the Lord: Ask now among the nations: Who has heard such fearful things which virgin Israel has done exceedingly?' If the church from the nations asks among the nations, it will be said: Hear what fearful things virgin Israel has done. For let us compare the life of those who sinned with the life of those who turned and believed, and we will know that those did fearful things, killing 'the Lord of glory,' but these turned to him who was killed and died by those for the sins of the world.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A crushed earthen vessel cannot be repaired, unlike a potter's clay vessel, so God had the prophet crush an earthen jar before the people to show that the city was handed over to an incurable disaster.
comments.comment: … Earthen vessels, once crushed, cannot be repaired, because of the hardness the fire has produced in them once for all. But a potter's vessels are not earthenware; they are clay. So even when they are distorted, they can easily return to a second shape through the craftsman's skill. When Scripture speaks of an incurable disaster, it does not say 'a potter's vessel' but 'an earthen vessel.' For example, when God wanted to teach the prophet and the Jews that He had handed the city over to an incurable disaster, He commanded him to take an earthen jar, crush it before all the people, and say, 'So shall this city be destroyed and crushed' (Jeremiah 19:10-11). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the prophet breaks an earthen jar rather than reshaping clay.
comments.author: John Chrysostom

comments.capsule: Scripture takes care to say who Pashhur was and where the pit was, and that Pashhur, who struck and threw Jeremiah into it, is given a new name, Migrant, and his friends will fall by a sword of their enemies.
comments.comment:
Jeremiah prophesied, and Pashhur son of Immer the priest heard the words of the prophecy. And though, as is likely upon the bare sequence of the prophecy, many had heard Jeremiah, it is not quickly written that another heard except Pashhur. And Scripture cared to say also whose son he was—that of Immer—and that he was called a priest, and what rank he had among the people—that he had been appointed leading the house of the Lord at the time Jeremiah was prophesying these words.

And it is written that hearing the words of this prophecy Pashhur struck Jeremiah, and was not content with having struck him, but also threw him into a certain fall-pit. Scripture cared to say also where this fall-pit was—in the gate of Benjamin—and that the fall-pit was in a place where there was an upper room, and an upper room of no other than the house of the Lord. These things the Holy Spirit wrote as having come to be upon the prophecy to Jeremiah, and as having come from Pashhur.

Then it says: on the next day Pashhur led Jeremiah out of the fall-pit. And led out, Jeremiah said to Pashhur that the Lord did not call you this name Pashhur; another name has been set for you—as for Jacob, Israel; as for Abram, Abraham; as for Sarai, Sarah—so he has set for you the name Migrant. And for this reason he called you Migrant, because the Lord says: Behold, I give you into migration with all—with whom? Not with your wife and your sons and your daughters, but with your friends. And when you are given into migration, your friends will fall by a sword. Then, as there is a difference for those falling by a sword if they fall by a sword of enemies or by a sword of others, he says that the friends of the one who threw Jeremiah into the fall-pit will fall into a sword of their enemies. And your eyes, he says, will see these things prophesied. But you and all Judah I will give into the hands of the king of Babylon, after your friends suffer these things, and they will migrate them into Babylon and will cut them down; for the king of Judah and those from Judah they will cut down with a sword, and no longer is 'of their enemies' added, as upon the former who were said to be friends of Pashhur. Then he says: and I will give all the strength of this city and all the treasures of the king of Judah and all the labors of this city into the hands of their enemies …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet Jeremiah is struck as Paul was, and Jesus is seen still giving his back to scourges, in the blasphemies and plots of unbelievers against the Word of God.
comments.comment:
… So then Pashhur 'struck Jeremiah the prophet,' and with character: 'and he struck Jeremiah the prophet.' (Jeremiah 20:2) 'The prophet' is also added. Here then the one who struck Jeremiah the prophet.

And it is written in Acts that someone struck Paul, ordered by Ananias the high priest. Therefore Paul said: 'God is about to strike you, whitewashed wall.' (Acts 23:3) And until now Ebionites, ordered by an unlawful high-priestly word, strike the apostle of Jesus Christ with blasphemous words. And Paul says toward such a high-priestly word: 'God is about to strike you.' And such a high priest is handsome on the surface and a whitewashed wall.

Christ says: 'I have given my back to scourges, and my cheeks to blows, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spit.' (Isaiah 50:6) The simple know these things only of that time when Pilate scourged him, when Jews planned against him. But I see Jesus daily 'giving his back to scourges.' Go into the synagogues of the Jews and see Jesus scourged by them with the tongue of blasphemy. See those gathered from the nations planning against Christians, how they take Jesus, and there too he 'gives his own back to scourges.' Consider the Word of God being insulted, spoken ill of, hated by the unbelievers. See that 'he gave his cheeks to blows,' and having taught that if someone strikes you on the cheek turn also the other, he himself does it. So many strike and scourge him, and he is silent and does not speak. For it is written that he does not speak when being scourged. And 'until now Jesus has not turned his face away from the shame of spit.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The prophet is thrown into the pit of the upper room because the temple stood in Benjamin's allotment, and the upper room stands for the high and lifted mind where holy ones received the prophets.
comments.comment:
It followed upon the prophet having been struck to narrate those struck—for example the apostle and if anyone else has been struck—and to set beside them also the things about Jesus himself. So 'Pashhur struck Jeremiah the prophet and threw him into the fall-pit which was in the Benjamin gate of the upper room.' (Jeremiah 20:2) The fall-pit of Benjamin was of the upper room. Benjamin’s allotment is Jerusalem, in which is the temple of God, as the one able to hear the divine readings will find from the allotment written in Joshua. Since then the temple was in Benjamin’s allotment, which is interpreted Son of the right hand (for there is nothing leftward about the temple of God), for this reason this one throws 'into the fall-pit which was in the Benjamin gate of the upper room of the Lord’s house.' (Jeremiah 20:2) While there is an 'upper room in the Lord’s house' he 'threw' the prophet 'into the fall-pit.'

And we beg that taking Jeremiah now we may bring him up into the upper room 'in the Lord’s house.' And I will show from Scripture that the upper room is the high and lifted mind, when it bears witness to the holy ones that they received the prophets into upper rooms. In the third of Kingdoms a widow receiving Elijah the prophet in Zarephath of Sidon lodged the prophet 'into her upper room.' And in the fourth the one receiving Elisha prepared a house for him into the upper room. But sinful Ahaziah fell from the upper room. And Jesus also commands you not to come down from the housetop. For he says: when these and these things happen, 'then let the one on the housetop not come down to take the things from his house.' (Matthew 24:17) The one fleeing in persecutions is not told not to go up onto a housetop, but from the housetop 'not to come down to take the things from his house.'

It is good then to be in upper rooms, good to be on housetops and somehow to be above. And the wonderful apostles also, as is written of them in Acts, when being together they were free for prayers and the word of God, were in an upper room. And since they were in an upper room, they were not below. For this reason 'tongues as of fire distributed appeared to them.' But Peter also, when he was sending up the prayer to God, 'went up onto the housetop'; and if he had not gone up onto the housetop, he would not have seen 'a vessel as a sheet coming down from heaven, let down by four corners from heaven.' …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The sinner throws the prophet into the pit while this age lasts, but on the next day Pashhur is given into migration to Babylon with his friends, and whoever sins is handed over to the king of Babylon, who in the ascent is the evil one.
comments.comment:
'And it came to be on the next day, and Pashhur led Jeremiah out of the fall-pit.' (Jeremiah 20:3) O Lord Jesus, come again; make these things clear also to me and to those who have come upon the spiritual food. How on 'the next day' does he himself lead 'Jeremiah out of the fall-pit'? For as long as today’s day stands—and today is this whole age—the sinner throws the prophet down into the fall-pit; but if the present day ceases and tomorrow comes, then having repented he leads him out from the fall-pit.

Then Jeremiah says to him what Pashhur will suffer. What does he say to him? 'Not Pashhur did he call your name, but Migrant. For thus says the Lord.' (Jeremiah 20:3) This Pashhur is about to be migrated according to the worth of the sins into Babylon—not alone, but also with his friends. For he is handed over to Nebuchadnezzar and goes away into Confusion and is punished for his sins, since 'he threw the prophet into the fall-pit.' (Jeremiah 20:2) Who then are the friends of Pashhur, the namesake of Blackness of mouth? All who have received his words, who have been blackened together with his blackened mouth, who have received doctrines of blackness. 'And they will fall by a sword of their enemies.' (Jeremiah 20:4) Those appointed over punishments—these are the ones who have the swords and make them fall; concerning whom the word prophesies and says: 'And your eyes will see.' These prophesied things, he says, 'your eyes will see.'

'And you and all Judah I will give into the hands of the king of Babylon.' Whoever of Judah is caught so sinful as to be worthy of the king of Babylon, of Confusion, will be handed over to him. And the king of Babylon receives those who sin. And the king of Babylon according to the history is Nebuchadnezzar, but according to the ascent is the evil one. And to this one the sinner is handed over, since he is both enemy and avenger. And that the sinner is handed over to him, let Paul teach you, where on the one hand he says about Hymenaeus and Alexander: 'whom I handed over to Satan,' and about the one who has fornicated: 'when you are gathered and my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus, I have judged to hand over such a one to Satan for destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: What Scripture says of God's wrath, anger and regret shares only the name with ours, for his wrath educates those whom his word has not educated, and each is worthy of the good God.
comments.comment:
All the things written about God, even if they look discordant at first hearing, must be understood as worthy of the good God. Who will not say that things referred to God—that he has wrath, that he uses anger, that he regrets, even that he sleeps—look discordant? But each of these, for the one who knows how to hear dark words, will be found worthy of God.

For his wrath is not barren: as his word educates, so also his wrath educates; those not educated by word he educates by wrath. And it is necessary that God use the so-called wrath as he uses the so-named Word; for his Word is not such as everyone’s word. No one’s word is 'a living being,' no one’s word is 'God,' no one’s word was 'in the beginning' toward that one whose the Word was. So also God’s wrath is called wrath not as just anyone’s wrath. And as the Word of God has something strange beside every word of just anyone—being God, being Word as living, existing by itself, serving the Father—so once God’s so-called wrath was named, it has something strange and alien to every defined wrath.

So also his anger has something of its own; for it belongs to the purpose of the anger that refutes, wanting the one refuted to turn through the refutation. Word also refutes, as word educates; but word does not refute as anger refutes. Those not benefited by the refutation from the word will need the refutation from the anger. We said there is also a regret of God that looks discordant at first glance, since it is written: 'I have regretted that I anointed Saul as king.' (1 Samuel 15:11) Worthily seek also the regret, and do not think his regret has kinship with the regret of those who regret. As his Word had something exceptional, and his wrath something surpassing, and nothing was akin to these among the like-named, so also his regret is like-named with our regret; and like-named are those whose name alone is common, but the account of the substance according to the name is other. Therefore only the name is common of God’s anger and anyone’s anger, and only the name of anyone’s wrath and God’s wrath. So also upon regret. And the one able will seek what God’s regret works, what it worked. It took down Saul reigning lawlessly; it raised as king for the people the one according to God’s heart; for he said because of that good regret: 'I have found a man according to my heart, David son of Jesse.' (Acts 13:22) But all these things are a preface for me (Jeremiah 20:7).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God, who persuades and does not force, deceived Jeremiah by telling him he would carry a cup of wrath to all the nations, so that he was deceived, not suspecting that Israel also would drink from it.
comments.comment:
For we seek whether, as everyone’s anger is evil but God’s is refuting, and everyone’s wrath is harsh but God’s so-called wrath is educative, and our regret accuses weakness in the one before the regret, but upon God his regret does not accuse God but the outward affairs upon which the regret is taken—so also one must understand the deception of God as of another kind beside our deception with which we deceive. What then is the deception beside God’s, which the prophet understood when he ceased being deceived, and says, knowing the benefit from having been deceived: 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived' (Jeremiah 20:7)?

And first I will use a Hebrew tradition that has come to us through someone who fled because of the faith of Christ and because of having gone up from the law and having come where we spend time. He told either a story that appears or a word able to lead the hearers to 'You deceived me, Lord, and I was deceived.' (Jeremiah 20:7) He said such things: God does not tyrannize but reigns, and reigning he does not force but persuades, and wants those under him to offer themselves willingly to his economy, that someone’s good may not be according to necessity but according to the willing. Which Paul also knowing said in the letter to Philemon about Onesimus: 'that your good may not be according to necessity but according to willing.' (Philemon 1:14) The God of all could then make a supposed good in us, that of necessity we give alms and of necessity be temperate, but he has not wished it. Therefore he does not command us to do what we do from grief or from necessity, that what comes to be may be willing. He seeks a way, so to speak, how someone may willingly do what God wants.

The tradition then also told me something such: he wanted to send Jeremiah to prophesy to all the nations and before all the nations to the people. But since the prophecies had something more gloomy—for they announced punishments which each according to worth will be punished—and he knew the prophet’s choice not wanting to prophesy the worse things to the people of Israel, for this reason he managed to say: 'Take this cup, and you will make all the nations drink to whom I will send you.' … God then commanded Jeremiah to take a cup, and urging him upon taking the cup of the unmixed wine he says he will send him to all the nations having this cup. And Jeremiah hearing that he is sent to all the nations to serve a cup of wrath, a cup of punishments, not suspecting that Israel also is about to drink from the cup of punishment, was deceived.
comments.selected_reason: Gives a clear account of what it means that God deceived the prophet.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God deceives for our benefit, as a father hides his love under threats toward an infant son and a physician hides the cutting iron under a sponge and the bitter drug under honey.
comments.comment:
… Perhaps then, as a father wants to deceive a son still an infant for benefit—who cannot otherwise be benefited unless the child is deceived—as a physician practices deceiving the sick person who cannot be healed unless he accepts words of deception, so also the God of all, since he has set before him to benefit the race of humans. Let the physician say to the sick: You must be cut, you must be cauterized, you must suffer other harder things; that one would not offer himself. But sometimes he says something else, and hid under the sponge that cutting, dividing iron, and again hides under the honey the nature of the bitter and unpleasant drug, wanting not to harm but to heal the one being treated. Of such drugs the whole divine Scripture is full. And some are useful things hidden, some are bitter things hidden.

If you see a father threatening as if hating the son and saying fearful things to the son and not displaying affection but hiding the love toward the son, you will see that he wants to deceive the infant; for it does not benefit the son to know the father’s love; he will be relaxed and will not be educated. For this reason he hides the sweet of affection, shows the bitter of the threat. Something such God does from the analogy of father and physician. There are bitter things which heal even the most just and the wisest; for everyone who has sinned must be punished for the sins. 'Do not be deceived; God is not mocked.' (Galatians 6:7) Whether fornicator or adulterer or soft or male-bedder or thief or drunkard or reviler or plunderer, they will not inherit God’s kingdom. If this is understood exactly by those unable to see the medical iron under the sponge, by those unable to understand the bitter drug under the honey, someone will grow weary. Which of us does not know himself as having drunk without counsel and become drunk? Which of us is clean from theft and from not providing the needed things as due? But see what the word says: 'Do not be deceived, that these will not inherit God’s kingdom.' (1 Corinthians 6:9–10)
comments.selected_reason: Gives the picture of the father and the physician to explain being deceived by God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: There is a promise of blessed laughter that goes with blessed weeping, and the teacher who grieves a sinner's soul leads him through weeping to the blessed laughter.
comments.comment:
'For with my bitter word I will laugh.' (Jeremiah 20:8) There is a promise of laughter, of which promise the patriarch Isaac is namesake; for he is interpreted Laughter. And that laughter is a promise is clear from 'Blessed are those who weep now'—and the promise is 'that they will laugh.' As there is a promise 'they will be called sons of God,' and 'they will see God,' and 'they will inherit the earth,' and 'theirs is the kingdom of the heavens,' (Matthew 5:9) so there is a promise of laughter; to which promise the opposite—for the one being blessed—is weeping.

And you will seek whether this good laughter, according to one and another sense, agrees with the blessed weeping, but is opposed by another weeping stored up for the opposites. For 'Woe to those who laugh now, for they will mourn and weep' (Luke 6:25)—one weeping is the blessed, another is stored up for those who have lived badly. And whether even that one has a beneficial end, I do not know. Hear Paul. That he taught, he worked at grieving the hearers. And he confesses that then especially he rejoiced when someone was grieved by him; for he says: 'And who is the one who makes me glad if not the one grieved by me?' (2 Corinthians 2:2) And if someone is able to move a hearer’s soul, especially one who has sinned, he prays to speak such words which, announced from power and array and divinity and sacred thoughts, will shake the hearer’s soul and move it unto mourning and unto weeping and unto tears, so that the speaker rejoices when he sees the hearing turned and filled upon what is said. For where he leads unto promises, as through the narrow and afflicted way in being grieved unto life, he also leads through weeping unto the blessed laughter. But when he does not accomplish this, I fear lest he say such things: 'Woe to those who laugh now, for you will mourn and weep.' …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Jeremiah is reproached only for the word of the Lord, and honestly records his human sin of vowing not to name the Lord's name, but the word became a burning fire in his heart.
comments.comment:
'Because the word of the Lord became for me a reproach.' (Jeremiah 20:8) Blessed Jeremiah having no other reproach except the word of the Lord. But we wretched ones have reproaches not because of the word of the Lord but because of our own sins, and we are reproached for what we stumble in, and we are reviled for our evils. And the Savior does not want us to be reproached with such reproaches, saying: 'Blessed are you when they reproach you and persecute you and say every evil word against you because of me. Rejoice in that day and leap.' (Matthew 5:11) The word of the Lord then, he says, became for me a reproach and a mockery every day.

Then understand how the prophets are well-minded humans and do not hide their own sins as we also do, speaking not only for those then but for all generations if they have sinned. And I hesitate to confess my sins before the few here, since the hearers are about to condemn me. But Jeremiah, having suffered something sinful, was not ashamed, but wrote up his own sin; for it was a sin, what follows in: 'And I said: I will by no means name the name of the Lord, and I will by no means speak still upon his name.' (Jeremiah 20:9) You were taught to do all things in the Lord’s name; and you say you will not name the Lord’s name? But what name will you name? 'You shall not remember the name of other gods in your hearts,' and you say this? He says then having suffered something human, which we also often risk. Especially if someone knows himself as having been miserable because of teaching and the word and having suffered and been hated, he often says: I withdraw; what to me and affairs? If from teaching I am in affairs, why do I not rather withdraw to desert and quiet? Something such the prophet also suffered.

But upon this the Lord is good who prevents such sins of such great ones. He did not leave the prophet to make true what he said, but even in this he made Jeremiah call upon faithlessness and make faithless what was said. For he said he would no longer name the Lord’s name. 'And it became,' he says, 'in my heart as a fire burning, flaming in my bones, and I am exhausted from every side and cannot bear it.' The word of the Lord became burning his heart.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the prophet's reproach, his confessed lapse and the fire of the word.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We are told to weep not for the dead but for the one who has fallen from blessedness and eternal life, and a man may rightly mourn himself when he has become lost in sins.
comments.comment: … But the Savior does not bless those who mourn in just any way. For sometimes they also fall away, even while the word says: 'Do not weep for one dead, nor mourn him; but weep with a weeping for the one departing from the presence of the Lord, because he will not return again' (Jeremiah 22:10).
